domains.name: Reconnaissance & OSINT
domains.description: Passive and active reconnaissance: DNS, OSINT, scanning strategy — seeing your attack surface the way an adversary does.

scenarios.title: The Staging Server on crt.sh
scenarios.situation: During a self-assessment, you query crt.sh for your company's domain and find `staging-legacy.example.com` — a three-year-old staging host with a valid public certificate, still resolving, running an unpatched application. It was never in any asset inventory.
objectives: Treat unknown public assets as incidents
evidence: staging-legacy.example.com, cert valid, issued 2026-08-14; host responds on 443 with 200 OK.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct response?
choices: Ignore it — it's just a staging host and certificates are public anyway.
Treat it as an exposed asset: verify what's running, assess patching and access controls, and either decommission it or bring it under management immediately.
Revoke the certificate; that solves the exposure.
Block crt.sh at the corporate firewall.
scenarios.hint: A forgotten staging host appears in public certificate logs — what does that tell you about the real problem?
scenarios.why: B is correct. The certificate log merely revealed the exposure — the host itself is the problem: unpatched, unmanaged, publicly reachable, and absent from inventory. Revoking the cert (C) doesn't patch the app or remove the host; blocking crt.sh (D) hides the mirror while the exposure remains; A is negligence. Unknown-to-you internet-facing hosts are among the most common breach entry points.

scenarios.title: The Indexed Backup File
scenarios.situation: A dork against your company's domain returns `backup-2026-09.sql.gz` in an open directory listing — a full database dump, indexed by the search engine, downloadable by anyone. It was placed there 'temporarily' during a migration six weeks ago.
objectives: Use search operators for exposure hunting
evidence: backup-2026-09.sql.gz, 2.1 GB, indexed; directory listing enabled; file dated 6 weeks ago.
scenarios.prompt: What is the full remediation?
choices: Delete the file from the server.
Remove the file, request search-engine cache removal, rotate every credential in the dump, audit access logs for downloads, and add directory-listing checks to monitoring.
Rename the file so the dork no longer finds it.
Password-protect the directory.
scenarios.hint: A database dump sat publicly indexed for six weeks — why isn't 'delete the file' enough?
scenarios.why: B is correct. Deleting the file (A) leaves the indexed/cached copy and ignores the six-week exposure window — every credential in that dump must be treated as compromised. Renaming (C) or password-protecting (D) after the fact doesn't un-expose what was public. Full remediation covers removal, cache purging, credential rotation, access auditing, and prevention.

scenarios.title: The Exposed Database
scenarios.situation: Your Shodan monitor alerts: a MongoDB instance on your company's IP range is indexed with no authentication, containing what looks like customer data. It was spun up by a developer 'for testing' and exposed to the internet by a misconfigured security group.
evidence: MongoDB, no auth, 2.3M documents, first indexed 11 days ago.
scenarios.prompt: What is the immediate response?
choices: Restrict network access to the database immediately, assess what data was exposed, rotate affected credentials, and investigate access logs — then implement the guardrail (no public databases) that prevents recurrence.
Add a password to the database; that fixes it.
Shut down the developer's laptop.
Email the developer asking them to secure it when convenient.
scenarios.hint: Shodan finds your unauthenticated customer database on the public internet — what is the ordered response?
scenarios.why: A is correct and ordered: stop the bleeding (network restriction) first, then assess the breach (data exposure, log review), rotate, and finally fix the systemic cause — developers must not be able to create public databases. B leaves the exposure window unexamined; C punishes hardware; D treats an active data exposure as a convenience request.

scenarios.title: The Credential-Stuffing Wave
scenarios.situation: Monday morning: 40 employees report locked accounts. Auth logs show thousands of login attempts from foreign IPs using valid email addresses — and valid passwords. Investigation finds the passwords came from a breach of an unrelated consumer service where employees reused their corporate passwords.
objectives: Deploy MFA as the stuffing countermeasure
evidence: 12,000 failed logins in 6h from 400 IPs; 37 accounts compromised via valid reused passwords.
scenarios.prompt: What breaks this attack chain structurally?
choices: Force a password reset for everyone and move on.
Enforce MFA on all accounts (so stolen passwords alone are useless), deploy breached-password detection at password-change time, and monitor for stuffing patterns.
Block all foreign IP addresses.
Ban employees from using the breached consumer service.
scenarios.hint: Breached passwords from an unrelated site are stuffing your logins — what structurally breaks the chain?
scenarios.why: B is correct. MFA is the structural fix — it makes the stolen password insufficient by itself. Breached-password detection prevents choosing known-compromised passwords, and stuffing monitoring catches the pattern early. A resets into the same vulnerable state; C is whack-a-mole (attackers use residential proxies); D doesn't address the reuse that already happened.

scenarios.title: The Scan That Set Off Every Alarm
scenarios.situation: A junior tester ran `nmap -A -p-` against the entire client /16 on day one of an engagement — full aggressive scan, all 65k ports, no phasing. The client's SOC called within the hour: the scan tripped every IDS, filled the SIEM, and the client is questioning the tester's professionalism. The scope authorized testing, but not like this.
evidence: 'port scan from tester IP across entire /16, all ports, aggressive mode' — 09:14, day 1.
scenarios.prompt: What should the scanning approach have been?
choices: Phased scanning: host discovery, then top ports on live hosts, then version detection on open ports, then targeted scripts — with timing appropriate to the engagement's stealth requirements.
Don't scan at all; just guess the services.
Scan faster with -T5 so it's over before the SOC notices.
Only scan port 80 to stay quiet.
scenarios.hint: An unphased aggressive /16 scan tripped every alarm — what is the professional scanning discipline?
scenarios.why: A is correct. Phasing minimizes noise while maximizing useful intelligence, and timing is matched to what the engagement requires (a red-team stealth test vs. an announced assessment differ). B abandons recon; C tries to outrun detection with more aggression — the opposite of professionalism; D misses everything except web servers.

scenarios.title: The Laptop with Five Clients' Reports
scenarios.situation: An assessor's laptop was stolen from a car. It contained unencrypted reports for five clients — including network diagrams, credentials found during tests, and unpatched vulnerability details. Full-disk encryption was 'on the to-do list.'
evidence: laptop stolen from vehicle; contained ~/clients/{a,b,c,d,e}/reports/ unencrypted.
scenarios.prompt: What is the incident response, and what should have prevented it?
choices: Notify all five clients immediately, treat found credentials as compromised (rotate), assess report sensitivity per client — and the prevention was full-disk encryption plus data destruction after engagement close.
Hope the thief just wants the hardware.
Change your own passwords; the clients' data is their problem.
Buy a new laptop and continue.
scenarios.hint: A stolen laptop held five clients' unencrypted test reports — what is the response and the prevention?
scenarios.why: A is correct. The response treats it as a multi-client breach: notification, credential rotation, sensitivity assessment. The prevention is layered — encryption makes the theft a hardware loss instead of a data breach, and engagement-close destruction minimizes what's on the disk at all. B, C, and D are all forms of hoping the problem away.

domains.name: Web Application Attacks
domains.description: How web apps fall: injection, XSS, auth attacks, SSRF/IDOR — and the defenses that stop each one.

scenarios.title: The Login Form That Talks Too Much
scenarios.situation: A tester types a single quote into the login's username field and gets: `You have an error in your SQL syntax near '' OR ...` — a raw MySQL error. The form also behaves differently for valid vs invalid usernames (different error messages).
evidence: single quote -> MySQL syntax error; valid user -> 'wrong password', invalid user -> 'user not found'.
scenarios.prompt: What do these observations indicate, and what is the fix?
choices: The app is vulnerable to SQL injection (raw errors prove unsanitized input reaches the DB) and leaks username validity (enumeration) — fix with parameterized queries and generic error messages.
The error message is just verbose; hide it and move on.
Add a CAPTCHA to the login form.
The different messages are helpful UX; keep them.
scenarios.hint: A quote in the login yields a raw SQL error — what are the two findings and the structural fix?
scenarios.why: A is correct on both findings: the SQL error proves input flows into query construction (injection), and distinct messages for valid/invalid users enable account enumeration. Parameterized queries cure the injection structurally; generic 'invalid credentials' messages cure the enumeration. B hides the symptom; C doesn't address either flaw; D preserves the enumeration oracle.

scenarios.title: The Comment That Stole Sessions
scenarios.situation: Users report being logged out mysteriously after viewing a forum thread. Investigation finds a comment containing `<script>` that harvests `document.cookie` and sends it to an external domain. The session cookies lack the HttpOnly flag. The comment has been viewed 12,000 times.
evidence: malicious comment live 36h, 12,041 views; session cookies without HttpOnly.
scenarios.prompt: What is the full response?
choices: Delete the comment and ban the user who posted it.

Remove the payload, force-rotate all session tokens, set HttpOnly+Secure+SameSite on cookies, add output encoding to the comment renderer, deploy a CSP, and investigate the 12,000 views for compromised sessions.
Tell users not to click suspicious comments.
Disable the forum temporarily.
scenarios.hint: A stored XSS harvested sessions from 12,000 views — what does complete remediation look like?
scenarios.why: B is correct and complete: the 12,000 views mean sessions are already stolen (rotate tokens, hunt for misuse), and the fixes must be structural (encoding everywhere, CSP, cookie flags) — not just deleting one payload. A treats it as a moderation issue; C blames users; D is downtime without remediation.

scenarios.title: The Spray That Lockout Didn't Catch
scenarios.situation: Auth logs show 50,000 login attempts overnight: 3 passwords tried against 16,000 accounts each, from rotating residential IPs. Per-account lockout never triggered (only 3 attempts per account). Nine accounts were compromised — all without MFA.
scenarios.prompt: What happened, and what stops it structurally?
choices: Password spraying evaded per-account lockout; the structural fix is MFA everywhere plus behavioral detection (many accounts, few passwords) and breached-password screening.
Lower the lockout threshold to 2 attempts.
Block residential IP ranges.
Require longer passwords.
scenarios.hint: 50,000 attempts, 3 passwords × 16,000 accounts, lockout never fired — what is this and what stops it?
scenarios.why: A is correct. This is textbook password spraying — designed to stay under per-account thresholds — and only the non-MFA accounts fell, proving MFA is the structural countermeasure. Behavioral detection catches the pattern that per-account counters miss. B would lock out legitimate users constantly; C is unmaintainable whack-a-mole; D doesn't help when the passwords are breached-valid.

scenarios.title: The Invoice Anyone Could Read
scenarios.situation: A customer reports seeing another company's invoice by changing `invoice_id=1042` to `1043` in the URL. The app requires login, and the invoices contain pricing and PII. The IDs are sequential. The feature 'worked fine in testing' because testers only ever viewed their own invoices.
evidence: invoice_id=1043 (another tenant) rendered fully for authenticated user of tenant A.
scenarios.prompt: What is the vulnerability and the fix?
choices: IDOR — missing server-side authorization: the fix is verifying `invoice.owner == current_user` on every object access (plus unguessable IDs as defense in depth).
The IDs should be encrypted in the URL.
Hide the invoice IDs from the page source.
It's fine — customers wouldn't guess other IDs.
scenarios.hint: Changing an invoice ID in the URL shows another company's data — what failed and what fixes it?
scenarios.why: A is correct. Authentication without per-object authorization is the IDOR pattern: the app knows who you are but never checks whether the object is yours. The ownership check is the cure; unguessable IDs raise the bar but don't fix the missing check. B and C are obscurity; D is the exact assumption attackers violate.

scenarios.title: The Grade-F Report Card
scenarios.situation: A client's public app scores F on securityheaders.com: no CSP, no HSTS, no X-Frame-Options. Last month's phishing campaign iframed the login page inside an attacker site (clickjacking) to harvest credentials. The app code itself was never breached.
objectives: Use WAF as defense in depth
evidence: securityheaders.com: F; missing CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options.
scenarios.prompt: What is the remediation priority?
choices: Rewrite the application's authentication system.
Deploy the header set (CSP, HSTS, frame-ancestors/X-Frame-Options, nosniff, referrer policy) — cheap, high-value, and directly prevents the clickjacking and downgrade classes.
Buy a WAF; headers are obsolete.
Take the login page offline.
scenarios.hint: No security headers, login page clickjacked via iframe — what is the highest-value fix?
scenarios.why: B is correct. The incidents (clickjacking, potential downgrade) are exactly the classes these headers prevent, and deployment is hours of config — not a rewrite. A is disproportionate (auth wasn't breached); C skips the cheaper fix and WAFs don't replace headers; D is availability destruction.

scenarios.title: The Profile Picture That Was PHP
scenarios.situation: A user uploaded 'profile.jpg' — actually PHP code with a JPG extension. The app stored it in `/uploads/` under the web root and served it back. Requesting `/uploads/profile.jpg` executed the code as the web user, giving the attacker a shell. The app 'validated' the extension.
evidence: /uploads/profile.jpg executed as PHP; attacker had web-user shell for 6h.
scenarios.prompt: Which controls, layered, prevent this?
choices: Content validation by parsing (not extension), randomized filenames, storage outside the web root, and safe serving headers — any two break the chain, all four is the standard.
Block the word 'php' in filenames.
Only allow uploads from admins.
Rename all uploads to .txt.
scenarios.hint: An uploaded 'JPG' executed as PHP from the web root — which layered controls break this chain?
scenarios.why: A is correct. The attack needs every link: bypass validation → predictable web-accessible path → execution on request. Breaking any link stops it; the four-layer standard is defense in depth. B is filterable a thousand ways; C abandons the feature; D breaks legitimate use and doesn't stop polyglots served with the wrong content type.

domains.name: Privilege Escalation & Persistence
domains.description: How attackers go from foothold to root — and how defenders spot each technique. Know it to kill it.

scenarios.title: The SUID Find Binary
scenarios.situation: During a hardening review you find `/usr/bin/find` is SUID root on a fleet of web servers — set by a configuration management error months ago. `find . -exec /bin/sh \;` gives a root shell to any local user, including the web application account.
evidence: /usr/bin/find SUID root on 214 web servers; set by CM 4 months ago.
scenarios.prompt: What is the severity and the fix?
choices: Critical — any local foothold becomes root trivially. Remove the SUID bit fleet-wide, audit for other SUID/capability drift, and investigate whether it was exploited during the exposure window.
Low — attackers would need a foothold first.
Just remove it from the one server you checked.
Document it as accepted risk.
scenarios.hint: SUID find on web servers — any local user gets root. Severity and response?
scenarios.why: A is correct. SUID find is a textbook GTFOBins root escalation — severity is critical because web shells and low-priv users are common footholds. The fix is fleet-wide (config management errors replicate), plus drift auditing (how else did it change?) and a lookback (was the window exploited?). B inverts the threat model; C ignores the fleet; D accepts a trivial root hole.

scenarios.title: The .env in the Backup
scenarios.situation: A backup script copies `/srv/app/` nightly to a world-readable archive share — including `.env` with production database credentials and API keys. The archives go back 90 days. The backup was set up 'temporarily' by someone who left.
evidence: .env with prod DB creds + 4 API keys in 90 daily archives, share readable by 'Everyone'.
scenarios.prompt: What is the full remediation?
choices: Fix the backup permissions and move on.

Rotate every credential in the .env (90-day exposure to everyone with share access), fix the backup to exclude secrets or encrypt it, restrict the share, audit access logs, and find who accessed the archives.
Delete the old archives; the current .env is fine.
Ask the former employee if they still have access.
scenarios.hint: Production credentials sat in world-readable backups for 90 days — what does full remediation require?
scenarios.why: B is correct. Ninety days of world-readable credential exposure means every secret in that file is compromised — rotation is non-negotiable. Then fix the mechanism (exclude/encrypt secrets in backups, restrict the share) and investigate the window (who read the archives?). A and C leave live compromised credentials in place; D is irrelevant.

scenarios.title: The Key That Survived the Password Reset
scenarios.situation: After a suspected compromise, the team reset all passwords and declared the incident closed. Two weeks later, the attacker is back — via an SSH key appended to a service account's `authorized_keys` during the original intrusion. Nothing in the IR checklist covered persistence mechanisms.
evidence: attacker key in svc-deploy's authorized_keys, added during initial intrusion, never reviewed.
scenarios.prompt: What should the IR process have included?
choices: A persistence review: authorized_keys for all accounts, cron jobs, systemd services/timers, and startup locations — password resets alone never evict an established attacker.
Stronger passwords for the next reset.
MFA on SSH (which wouldn't have stopped the key).
Reinstalling the SSH daemon.
scenarios.hint: Attacker returned after a full password reset via authorized_keys — what did IR miss?
scenarios.why: A is correct. The attacker survived because persistence mechanisms are independent of passwords — the IR process must explicitly enumerate and clear them. B repeats the failed response; C is good hygiene but key-based auth bypasses password MFA in many configs (and doesn't remove the key); D is theater.

scenarios.title: The 'No Malware Found' Breach
scenarios.situation: EDR found no malware on the compromised host — yet data was exfiltrated. Timeline shows: a phishing doc spawned PowerShell, which used `certutil` to download a script, executed it in memory via `IEX`, and exfiltrated via DNS queries. Every binary involved ships with Windows.
evidence: winword.exe -> powershell.exe -enc ... -> certutil -urlcache -> DNS exfiltration; zero malware hashes.
scenarios.prompt: Why did signature-based detection fail, and what detects this?
choices: The tools are legitimate OS binaries with no malicious hash — detection must be behavioral: parent-child anomalies (doc→PowerShell), encoded command lines, and unusual tool usage, via Sysmon/EDR rules.
The EDR needs better signatures.
Block certutil on all hosts.
The phishing doc should have been quarantined — endpoint is fine.
scenarios.hint: No malware found, but PowerShell+certutil exfiltrated data — why did signatures fail and what works?
scenarios.why: A is correct. Living-off-the-land means there's nothing to signature — the detection surface is behavior: who spawned what, with what arguments. Sysmon process-creation logging with rules for these patterns is the standard answer. B misunderstands the technique; C breaks legitimate admin use; D addresses one vector while the technique class remains.

scenarios.title: The Unquoted Service Path
scenarios.situation: A vulnerability scan flags `VulnApp Service` with binary path `C:\Program Files\VulnApp\bin\service.exe` (unquoted) running as SYSTEM. The `C:\Program Files\VulnApp` directory is writable by authenticated users.
evidence: VulnApp Service SYSTEM, unquoted path, dir writable by Authenticated Users.
scenarios.prompt: What is the exploit path and the fix?
choices: On boot, Windows tries `C:\Program.exe` before the real path — but the real vector here is simpler: the directory is writable, so replace/plant the service binary itself; it runs as SYSTEM. Fix: quote the path AND lock down directory DACLs so only admins can write.
It's just a scanner false positive; service paths don't matter.
Restart the service; that clears it.
Uninstall the application.
scenarios.hint: SYSTEM service, unquoted path, writable directory — what is the exploit and the complete fix?
scenarios.why: A is correct on both the exploit (writable directory + SYSTEM service = binary replacement, no path trickery even needed) and the complete fix (quoting alone wouldn't help since the directory is writable — both must be fixed). B dismisses a real SYSTEM vector; C changes nothing; D may be disproportionate if the app is needed — fix the config.

scenarios.title: The CI Container with the Socket
scenarios.situation: The CI system runs build jobs in containers — each mounted with `/var/run/docker.sock` 'so builds can build images.' A compromised dependency in one build job now has the Docker socket. The team says 'but it's just a container.'
evidence: all build pods mount /var/run/docker.sock; jobs run as root.
scenarios.prompt: What is the actual blast radius, and the fix?
choices: Host-root equivalent: the socket allows launching a privileged container with the host filesystem mounted — the 'contained' build job owns the CI host. Fix: remove socket mounts (use Kaniko/socket-proxy patterns), scope capabilities, run builds as non-root.
It's contained; the blast radius is the one container.
Just rotate the CI credentials.
Add a firewall rule.
scenarios.hint: Build containers mount the Docker socket — what is the blast radius?
scenarios.why: A is correct. The Docker socket is a root-equivalent API — 'just a container' with the socket mounted is a fiction; the escape to host root is one API call. The fix removes the mount entirely (there are purpose-built patterns for image builds that don't need it) and applies the container hardening checklist. B trusts the breached boundary; C and D don't address the escape path.

domains.name: Social Engineering
domains.description: The human attack surface: phishing, pretexting, vishing — and building the human firewall that resists them.

scenarios.title: The CEO's Urgent Request
scenarios.situation: Finance receives an email from the CEO: 'I'm in back-to-back meetings — please wire $48,000 to this vendor today, details attached. Don't call, I'm unreachable.' The tone is off, the vendor is new, and the reply-to is a Gmail address. The CFO is asking whether to 'just do it, it's the CEO.'
evidence: reply-to: ceo.name@gmaiI.com (capital i); vendor account opened 6 days ago.
scenarios.prompt: What is this, and what is the correct response?
choices: Business email compromise (BEC): do not wire — verify out-of-band via a known number, and treat any 'don't call me' instruction as the primary red flag.
It's probably legitimate; CEOs are busy. Wire it.
Reply asking for confirmation (to the same email).
Wire half now as a compromise.
scenarios.hint: An 'urgent, don't call me' wire request arrives from the CEO's lookalike address — what is it and what do you do?
scenarios.why: A is correct. This is textbook BEC: authority + urgency + secrecy ('don't call') + new payment details. The 'don't call' instruction exists precisely to prevent the verification that would kill the scam — so out-of-band verification via a independently-known number is mandatory. B, C (verifying with the attacker), and D all send money to criminals.

scenarios.title: The Helpdesk Password Reset
scenarios.situation: A caller to the helpdesk knows the ticket system name, the caller's manager's name, and references a real office move. They ask the analyst to reset a VIP's password and read back the temporary one. The analyst complies — it's the CEO's account.
evidence: no ticket existed; temp password read aloud; account was the CEO's.
scenarios.prompt: What failed, and what is the fix?
choices: Verification failed: the procedure must require ticket-first handling, callback to a directory number, and no verbal password readouts — self-service reset links instead.
The analyst needs better instincts.
Caller ID should be checked.
VIP accounts shouldn't exist.
scenarios.hint: A caller with perfect internal details social-engineers a VIP password reset — what process stops this?
scenarios.why: A is correct. Every 'verifiable' detail the caller knew was public OSINT — the process must not treat public facts as authentication. Ticket-first, callback verification, and eliminating verbal password readouts remove the attack's mechanics. B blames the human for a process failure; C is spoofable; D misses the point.

scenarios.title: The Printer Technician
scenarios.situation: 'I'm here to service the big printer on 3,' says the visitor with a toolbox and a confident smile. Reception waves him through — no badge check, no escort, no ticket. He spends 40 minutes on the floor, plugs a small device into a network jack behind the printer, and leaves. The device is found weeks later.
evidence: planted 3 weeks ago; captured LAN traffic including credentials in cleartext protocols.
scenarios.prompt: What failed at each layer?
choices: Visitor verification (no identity/ticket check), escort policy (unescorted access), and network access control (an unknown device got a LAN IP) — fix all three: verify + escort visitors, 802.1X on all ports.
Reception needs to be more suspicious of everyone.
Ban toolboxes.
The printer contract should be cancelled.
scenarios.hint: A fake technician planted a network device behind a printer — which three controls failed?
scenarios.why: A is correct. Three independent failures compounded: no verification, no escort, no network authentication — any one control would have blunted the attack. The fix is layered because the attack was layered. B is a vibe, not a control; C and D are absurd.

scenarios.title: The Unreported Phish
scenarios.situation: A real credential-harvesting phish hit 200 employees. Eight clicked and entered credentials. Zero reported it — the phish button was buried three menus deep, and the last person who reported a phish got a lecture about 'wasting SOC time' on a false positive. The campaign ran for 9 hours before IT noticed.
objectives: Measure report rate as the KPI
evidence: phish delivered 08:00; first click 08:07; IT noticed 17:12 via user complaint to manager.
scenarios.prompt: What are the program failures?
choices: Reporting friction (buried button) plus a culture that punishes reporting — fix: one-click reporting, fast triage, and celebrated reporters; measure report rate as the KPI.
The eight clickers should be fired.
Better email filters would have stopped it.
Nine hours is acceptable detection time.
scenarios.hint: Eight clicked, zero reported, 9 hours undetected — what failed in the human firewall?
scenarios.why: A is correct. The technology didn't fail first — the human sensor network did, because reporting was hard and punished. Eight silent compromises over 9 hours is the cost. One-click reporting with fast, grateful triage turns employees into the fastest detection layer you have. B destroys trust; C helps but targeted phish bypass filters; D normalizes failure.

scenarios.title: The Video Call with the CFO
scenarios.situation: Finance joins a video call: the CFO and two colleagues discuss an 'urgent acquisition payment.' Faces, voices, mannerisms all check out. The CFO asks finance to wire $2M immediately and keep it confidential. Something feels slightly off about the lip sync.
evidence: participants' video streams showed generation artifacts; CFO was in flight with no connectivity.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct action?
choices: Wire it — it's the CFO on video with colleagues; lip sync glitches happen.
Do not act on the call alone: end politely, call the CFO on their known number, and require the code word / dual approval before any wire.
Ask them to hold up today's newspaper on camera.
Wire a small test amount first.
scenarios.hint: A video call with the CFO demands an urgent $2M wire — what is the deepfake-era response?
scenarios.why: B is correct. This matches the documented $25M deepfake pattern exactly — multi-participant synthetic calls are now a known attack. Only independent-channel verification (known number, code word) distinguishes real from synthetic; the call itself is untrustworthy by design now. A trusts the compromised medium; C is defeated by real-time generation; D sends real money to criminals.

scenarios.title: The Compliance Survey
scenarios.situation: An email 'from HR' asks everyone to complete a 'security compliance survey' — it name-drops the CEO's initiative, says '87% of your department already completed it,' warns the deadline is today, and links to a lookalike domain. Three influence principles are working at once.
evidence: from: hr-notices@examp1e-hr.com; link domain registered 2 days ago.
scenarios.prompt: Which principles, and what is the correct response?
choices: Authority (CEO/HR), social proof (87% did it), scarcity (deadline today) — verify via the real HR channel before clicking; report the phish.
It's from HR, so complete it quickly to be compliant.
Forward it to the team so nobody misses the deadline.
Complete it but use a fake name.
scenarios.hint: An 'HR survey' pulls authority, social proof, and scarcity at once — how do you respond?
scenarios.why: A is correct. Naming the levers breaks their power: authority is unverified (check the real HR channel), the social-proof statistic is attacker-supplied, and the deadline manufactures urgency. Verify-then-act plus reporting is the trained reflex. B complies with the attack; C spreads it; D still hands data to the attacker.

domains.name: Incident Response
domains.description: When prevention fails: the IR lifecycle, triage, containment, eradication, and evidence handling.

scenarios.title: The 2 AM Call with No Playbook
scenarios.situation: Ransomware detonates at 2 AM. There is no playbook, no IR retainer, backups haven't been tested in a year, and logs roll every 7 days. The team spends the first 4 hours arguing about whether to pay, who decides, and whether to call the FBI — while the ransomware spreads to the backup server.
evidence: 02:00 detonation; 02:00-06:00 debate; 06:00 backups found encrypted too.
scenarios.prompt: What preparation would have changed this night?
choices: A tested IR playbook (severity matrix, decision authority, comms plan), tested offline backups, adequate log retention, and tabletop exercises — preparation is the phase that happens before the incident.
Better antivirus would have stopped it.
Hire more IT staff.
Pay the ransom faster next time.
scenarios.hint: No playbook, untested backups, 7-day logs — ransomware spreads for 4 hours. What phase failed?
scenarios.why: A is correct. Every failure that night was a preparation failure: no decision authority (arguing about payment), no tested restores (backups encryptable), no retention (investigation blind). B is single-tool thinking; C doesn't fix process; D is surrender as strategy.

scenarios.title: The One Alert That Was Twelve Hosts
scenarios.situation: EDR flags one workstation for credential-dumping. The analyst isolates it, closes the ticket as 'contained,' and moves on. Three weeks later, the same attacker is found on eleven more hosts — they'd moved laterally on day one using a service account, and nobody checked the auth logs.
evidence: svc-backup authenticated to 11 additional hosts within 4h of patient zero.
scenarios.prompt: What triage discipline was missing?
choices: Scope expansion: from the initial host, check auth logs for lateral movement, EDR on touched hosts, and the intrusion vector — one alert is a starting point, never the scope.
The EDR should have caught all twelve.
Isolate workstations faster.
More EDR licenses.
scenarios.hint: One EDR alert closed as 'contained'; attacker was on twelve hosts via a service account — what was missed?
scenarios.why: A is correct. Triage that stops at the first indicator isn't triage — it's the opening line of a breach report. The auth-log expansion would have found the lateral movement on day one. B blames the tool for a process failure; C and D don't address the missed scope.

scenarios.title: Ransomware at 3 AM
scenarios.situation: Ransomware is encrypting the file server at 3 AM. The on-call engineer wants to pull the power to 'stop it.' The backup admin says the backups 'should be fine.' Nobody has imaged anything, and the C2 domains are still reachable from the network.
evidence: file server encrypting; backups last verified 6 months ago; variant unidentified.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct first-30-minutes sequence?
choices: Pull the power immediately — stopping encryption is all that matters.
EDR/network-isolate hosts (keep powered for memory forensics), block C2 at the perimeter, image memory and disk, verify offline backups before trusting them — then eradicate.
Pay the ransom quickly before the price doubles.
Restore from backup right away to minimize downtime.
scenarios.hint: Ransomware encrypting at 3 AM, no images taken, C2 still reachable — what is the ordered response?
scenarios.why: B is correct and ordered: isolation stops spread while preserving memory evidence (pulling power destroys encryption keys in RAM and forensic state), C2 blocking cuts command, imaging preserves the investigation, and backup verification precedes any restore (backups are the ransomware's second target). A destroys evidence; C funds crime before exhausting recovery; D may restore from encrypted backups.

scenarios.title: The Recurring Web Shell
scenarios.situation: A web shell was 'removed' three times — and reappeared three times. Each time, the team deleted the shell file and moved on. The fourth occurrence exfiltrated the customer database. Forensics later found the attacker's cron job and an SSH key, both untouched by the 'remediation.'

lessons.title: Linux Hardening — Core concepts
concepts: SSH hardening: stale SSH keys are persistent, unaudited access — the former employee's laptop may be long gone but the key still opens root. Hardening means: inventory listeners, remove what's unneeded, bind the rest to localhost or internal interfaces, and firewall what's left.
Remote access: fix the access need properly instead of opening the file to everyone.
Least privilege: scoped rules (exact commands), personal accounts, and password-required sudo give least privilege plus attribution — and clean revocation when the internship ends.
Patch management: the overwhelming majority of exploited vulnerabilities are known CVEs with available patches — 'patch fear' is how servers get owned.

lessons.title: Scripting — Core concepts
concepts: Bash safety: verifying a published checksum or signature (fetched separately) before executing is the minimum due diligence. curl|bash as a habit trains you to execute uninspected code as root — the exact behavior attackers rely on.

Idempotent scripts: automation that isn't idempotent becomes a liability: duplicate firewall rules, failed user creation, unpredictable state. Cron's minimal environment (bare PATH, no shell profile) breaks scripts that work interactively — absolute paths fix that.
Principle: unquoted, unchecked variables in rm -rf are how disasters happen: an empty $BACKUP_DIR turns the command into 'rm -rf /old/*' — or worse.

useradd auditor
example.walkthrough: Automation that isn't idempotent becomes a liability: duplicate firewall rules, failed user creation, unpredictable state. Check-before-change (iptables -C, id username) makes re-runs safe and convergent — the script describes desired state, not just actions. This is the foundational discipline behind all configuration management.

lessons.title: Cryptography Basics — Core concepts
concepts: Password hashing: hashing proves integrity and identity (this file hasn't changed); encryption provides confidentiality (only key holders can read).

Storage security: an attacker can sign anything with their own key; the security is in the key distribution (verified fingerprint, trusted introducer, prior secure exchange). Using the wrong primitive means the security property you wanted doesn't exist.
Hashing vs encryption: this confusion causes real design failures: hashed backups are still readable by everyone (hashing doesn't hide data); 'encrypted' passwords are recoverable.
Key management: real systems are hybrid: asymmetric crypto (slow, solves key distribution) exchanges a random symmetric key; symmetric crypto (fast) encrypts the bulk data.

lessons.title: Forensics Intro — Core concepts
concepts: Order of volatility: forensics discipline: preserve (memory first per order of volatility, then disk image), document the chain of custody, and analyze copies. Order of volatility governs triage: registers/cache → memory → network state → running processes → disk → logs → backups.

Evidence preservation: every action on a live suspect system alters evidence — and rebooting destroys memory-resident artifacts entirely. Evidence is only as strong as its handling story: cryptographic hashes prove the image hasn't changed since collection, contemporaneous notes prove what you did, and access logs prove who touched it.
File timestamps: one timestamp is a claim; corroborated timestamps are evidence.

Timestomping: the mismatch is the tell: atime/mtime are trivially set with touch, but ctime (inode change time) updates on any metadata change and can't be set arbitrarily — today's ctime exposes the timestomping.
File recovery: recovery means: stop writing to that disk immediately (image it), carve the image for log-format data, and check log forwarding/SIEM copies (attackers forget the remote copy).

example.walkthrough: The mismatch is the tell: atime/mtime are trivially set with touch, but ctime (inode change time) updates on any metadata change and can't be set arbitrarily — today's ctime exposes the timestomping. Forensic timestamp analysis cross-references all three plus external sources (logs, journal).

lessons.title: Passive Recon: DNS, WHOIS & Certificate Transparency
concepts: Reconnaissance is the first phase of any attack — and the first phase of any defense assessment. Passive recon gathers intelligence without touching the target's systems: DNS records, WHOIS data, certificate transparency logs, and archived web content. Because you never send the target a packet, passive recon is undetectable — which is exactly why defenders must assume adversaries have already done it.

DNS is a goldmine: A/AAAA records reveal infrastructure, MX records reveal mail providers (and thus phishing targets), TXT records leak SPF/DKIM configuration (and sometimes secrets), and zone transfers — where misconfigured — dump the entire zone. Tools like `dig`, `host`, and `dnsenum` automate enumeration; sublist3r and amass find subdomains via certificate transparency and search engines.

Certificate Transparency (CT) logs are public, append-only records of every publicly-trusted TLS certificate — including subdomains the organization never announced. `crt.sh` lets anyone query 'all certificates for *.example.com,' instantly revealing dev, staging, and internal hostnames. If it's in a public cert, assume attackers know it.

WHOIS and historical DNS (SecurityTrails, VirusTotal) reveal registrar data, name servers, and — critically — what the infrastructure looked like months ago. Old DNS records point at decommissioned-but-still-resolving hosts: the forgotten staging server is the classic initial foothold. Defenders should run this same recon against themselves quarterly.

example.code:
$ dig example.com ANY +short
93.184.216.34
$ dig example.com MX +short
10 mail.example.com.
$ dig example.com TXT +short
"v=spf1 include:_spf.example.net ~all"

# certificate transparency: subdomains nobody announced
$ curl -s 'https://crt.sh/?q=%25.example.com&output=json' | \
    jq -r '.[].name_value' | sort -u | head
dev.example.com
staging.example.com
vpn.example.com
example.walkthrough: The `dig` queries enumerate the target's public footprint: web IP, mail infrastructure, and SPF policy — all without touching the target beyond its public DNS servers. The crt.sh query against certificate transparency logs reveals dev, staging, and VPN hostnames the organization never published. An attacker now has a target list; the defender's job is to have found and secured these first.

pitfalls: Scanning before passive recon: active scanning is noisy and logged — exhaust passive sources first so your target list is precise before you ever send a packet.
Trusting WHOIS blindly: GDPR redaction and privacy services hide registrant data — treat WHOIS as one corroborating source, not ground truth.
Forgetting your own exposure: if you can crt.sh your org's forgotten staging host, so can everyone else — run this recon on yourself and kill what shouldn't be public.

lessons.title: Google Dorking & Search Operators
concepts: Search engines index far more than marketing pages: misconfigured servers expose directory listings, backup files, error messages with stack traces, and documents containing credentials. Google dorking uses advanced operators — `site:`, `filetype:`, `inurl:`, `intitle:`, `intext:` — to query that indexed exposure precisely. It's passive, legal on public data, and devastatingly effective.

The operator grammar: `site:example.com filetype:pdf` finds indexed PDFs on the domain; `inurl:admin intitle:login` finds login pages; `intext:'password' filetype:xls` finds spreadsheets mentioning passwords; the minus operator excludes (`-site:www.example.com`). Combining operators narrows from millions of results to the handful that matter.

The Google Hacking Database (GHDB) catalogs dorks by category — files containing passwords, vulnerable servers, exposed webcams, error messages. Defenders use it as a checklist: run the dorks against your own domains, and everything that returns a hit is a finding. 'We'd never expose that' is tested, not assumed.

Operational security for dorking: use it against your own assets or with authorization; aggressive automated dorking can trip rate limits and WAFs. And remember the meta-lesson — if a dork finds your `.env` backup in the index, the fix isn't just deleting the file, it's checking whether it was ever accessed and rotating everything it contained.

example.code:
site:example.com filetype:env
site:example.com inurl:phpinfo.php
site:example.com intitle:"index of" "parent directory"
filetype:sql intext:"INSERT INTO" site:example.com
inurl:/wp-content/uploads/ filetype:xls intext:password
example.walkthrough: Each line is a dork with a specific exposure in mind: environment files (which contain secrets), phpinfo pages (which leak configuration), open directory listings, dumped SQL databases, and spreadsheets mentioning passwords in upload directories. Run against your own domain, any hit is an immediate finding — these are the exact queries adversaries automate.

pitfalls: Dorking without authorization against third parties: passive but still reconnaissance — keep it to your own assets or scoped engagements.
Finding it and just deleting the file: the indexed copy may persist in caches, and the exposure window is unknown — rotate any exposed secrets and check access logs.
One-off dorking: exposures reappear with every deploy — automate the dork checklist in your security monitoring.
lessons.try_it: Run three GHDB-style dorks against a domain you own (or a test domain). For each hit, write the finding as: exposure, potential impact, remediation.

lessons.title: Shodan & Internet-Wide Scanning Data
concepts: Shodan continuously scans the entire IPv4 internet and indexes what it finds: open ports, service banners, screenshots of web interfaces, default credentials on IoT devices. It's a search engine for exposed infrastructure — query `port:22 country:US` and browse SSH servers; search your organization's IP ranges and see exactly what the internet sees.

The defensive workflow: search your own netblocks and ASN regularly. Every unexpected open port, every banner advertising an old version, every exposed database or webcam is a finding before an adversary catalogs it. Shodan even offers monitoring alerts for new exposures on your ranges — free continuous recon against yourself.

Banner analysis is the core skill: a banner like `SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_7.4` immediately tells an attacker the version and its known CVEs. Version-hiding (or better, patching) reduces this signal. Default credentials on the Shodan-indexed device turn information into access — the Mirai botnet was built on exactly this.

Shodan's data is historical too — it remembers what was exposed last month. 'We closed that port yesterday' doesn't erase the record that it was open, or the scans adversaries ran while it was. Exposure windows matter; assume anything ever exposed was catalogued.

example.code:
# what the internet sees (defensive self-check)
shodan search --fields ip_str,port,org "org:\"Example Corp\" port:3389"
# or via the web UI: net:203.0.113.0/24
#
# typical findings to act on:
#  - RDP/SSH open to the world (should be VPN-only)
#  - banners advertising EOL software versions
#  - databases (mongo/redis/elastic) with no auth
example.walkthrough: The Shodan query enumerates internet-facing RDP on the organization's range — each hit is a host the whole internet can also see. The findings list is the triage order: remote-access protocols exposed globally, version banners advertising exploitable software, and databases without authentication are the exposures adversaries convert to footholds first.

pitfalls: Searching Shodan once and forgetting: exposures appear with every deploy and config change — monitor continuously, alert on new exposures.
Exposing RDP/SSH to 0.0.0.0 'temporarily': Shodan indexes in hours; temporary becomes permanent in the scan data — use VPN/bastion from the start.
Ignoring historical data: closing the port today doesn't un-ring the bell — check what was exposed during the window and investigate.
lessons.try_it: Search Shodan for your home IP or a test range (free tier). List every open port found and write the hardening action for each.

lessons.title: People OSINT & Breach Data
concepts: People-focused OSINT assembles a target's digital footprint from public sources: social media, professional profiles, breached credential dumps, and public records. Attackers use it to craft convincing pretexts ('Hi, it's IT — I see you just got back from the conference in Austin...'). Defenders use it to understand what ammunition exists against their people.

Breach data is the highest-value source: `haveibeenpwned.com` lets anyone check whether an email appears in known breaches, and the associated password dumps fuel credential-stuffing attacks — automated login attempts using breached email/password pairs. Password reuse turns one breach into many compromises, which is why reused passwords are the attacker's favorite vulnerability.

The defensive program: monitor your domain on HIBP (domain-wide notifications), enforce MFA everywhere (so a stuffed password alone is useless), and run internal phishing simulations informed by real OSINT — if your test phish uses the CEO's actual LinkedIn details, employees learn what real targeting looks like.

Teach the personal lesson too: what employees post publicly (conference badges with QR codes, 'my first day' photos showing badge designs, vacation countdowns) becomes pretext material. OSINT awareness training with the employee's own public footprint is far more persuasive than generic slides.

example.code:
# check exposure (defensive, your own addresses)
# haveibeenpwned.com -> enter corporate email
# Result example: 'Found in 3 breaches: Collection#1, ...'
#
# organizational response:
# 1. force password reset for affected accounts
# 2. verify MFA is enabled on those accounts
# 3. hunt for logins using breached passwords (auth logs)
# 4. domain-wide HIBP monitoring going forward
example.walkthrough: The HIBP check is the starting point: an address in three breaches means three password dumps contain its credentials. The organizational response is mechanical — reset, verify MFA, hunt auth logs for stuffing attempts, then set up domain monitoring so the next breach triggers action automatically instead of being discovered by accident.

pitfalls: Checking HIBP once: new breaches appear constantly — domain monitoring makes it continuous.
Resetting passwords without enabling MFA: the next breach re-compromises the account — MFA is what breaks the stuffing chain.
Blaming the employee for being breached: breaches happen to services, not people — the failure is reuse and missing MFA, fix the system.
lessons.try_it: Check your own email addresses on HIBP. For each breach hit, confirm: is the password still in use anywhere, and is MFA on that account?

lessons.title: Active Recon: Nmap Scanning Strategy
concepts: Active recon sends packets to the target — port scans, service detection, OS fingerprinting. Nmap is the standard: `nmap -sS` (SYN scan, half-open, stealthier), `-sV` (service/version detection), `-O` (OS fingerprinting), `-A` (aggressive: all of the above plus scripts). Strategy matters more than flags: scan in phases, from broad to deep.

The phased approach: host discovery first (`-sn` ping sweep to find live hosts), then port scan the live hosts (top 1000 ports, then full 65535 on interesting ones), then version detection only on open ports, then targeted NSE scripts (`--script=vuln`) on specific services. Each phase narrows the next — you don't version-scan 65k ports on 254 hosts.

Timing and stealth are operational choices: `-T4` is fast and loud (fine for your own lab), `-T2`/`-T1` are slow and quiet (for avoiding IDS, with authorization). Fragmentation (`-f`) and decoys (`-D`) evade naive detection — know they exist so you recognize them in your own IDS logs, not so you can be sneaky without permission.

The golden rule: never scan what you don't own or lack written authorization to test. Unauthorized scanning violates CFAA in the US and equivalents elsewhere — 'I was just checking' is not a defense. In labs, scan your own VMs; in jobs, scan what's in the written scope. Everything else is theory until authorized.

example.code:
# phased scan strategy (your own lab network)
# phase 1: which hosts are alive?
nmap -sn 192.168.56.0/24
# phase 2: ports on live hosts
nmap -sS --top-ports 1000 192.168.56.101
# phase 3: versions on open ports only
nmap -sV -p 22,80,443 192.168.56.101
# phase 4: targeted vuln scripts
nmap --script=vuln -p 80,443 192.168.56.101
example.walkthrough: The four phases narrow the aperture at each step: ping sweep finds the live hosts (no point scanning empty addresses), SYN scan finds open ports on those hosts, version detection runs only against open ports, and vulnerability scripts target only the interesting services. Each phase's output focuses the next — efficient, and the minimum noise necessary for the intelligence gained.

pitfalls: Full `-A` scan of a /24 as step one: maximum noise, hours of output, and you've announced yourself to every IDS — phase from broad to narrow.
Scanning without written authorization: the CFAA doesn't care about your curiosity — own it, lab it, or scope it in writing.
Version-scanning 65k ports: `-sV` on every port of every host takes forever — version-detect open ports only.
lessons.try_it: Against your own lab VMs, run the four-phase sequence. Document: hosts found, open ports, service versions, and one NSE finding per host.

lessons.title: SQL Injection: From Tautology to Exfiltration
concepts: SQL injection happens when user input is concatenated into a SQL query without parameterization: the input stops being data and becomes code. The classic tautology `' OR '1'='1` turns `WHERE user='$input' AND pass='$pw'` into `WHERE user='' OR '1'='1' ...` — always true, so authentication is bypassed without knowing any password.

Beyond login bypass: UNION-based injection appends `UNION SELECT` to exfiltrate other tables' data through the application's own responses; error-based injection uses database error messages to reconstruct data; blind injection asks the database yes/no questions (timing or boolean responses) to extract data bit by bit when no output is visible. All three are the same root cause with different exfiltration channels.

The fix is structural, not filtering: parameterized queries (prepared statements) separate code from data at the database driver level — the input can never become SQL. `cursor.execute('SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?', (name,))` is safe by construction. Input validation and WAFs are defense-in-depth; parameterization is the cure. ORMs parameterize by default — raw SQL strings are where injection lives.

Testing for it (authorized only): a single quote in an input field that produces a database error message is the tell. Defenders should fuzz their own inputs, review every raw SQL string, and treat any string-concatenated query as a finding — even if 'nobody would think to try that input.'

example.code:
# VULNERABLE (string concatenation - the bug)
query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '" + user + "'"
# input: ' OR '1'='1  -->  WHERE username = '' OR '1'='1'

# SAFE (parameterized - the fix)
cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = ?", (user,))
# input is bound as DATA; it can never become SQL syntax
example.walkthrough: The vulnerable version interpolates user input directly into the SQL string — the attacker's quote breaks out of the string literal and the `OR '1'='1'` makes the WHERE clause universally true. The safe version passes the input as a bound parameter: the database driver sends code and data separately, so even a malicious input is treated as a literal string to compare, never as syntax to execute.

pitfalls: Blocklisting 'suspicious' keywords: attackers bypass filters with encoding, comments, and case tricks — parameterization doesn't care what the input contains.
'Our ORM handles it' while raw SQL lurks: one hand-written query with concatenation reopens the hole — audit every raw SQL string.
Relying on error-message hiding: suppressing errors converts error-based to blind injection — it slows attackers, it doesn't stop them; fix the query.
lessons.try_it: In a local lab app (e.g., DVWA or a scratch Flask app), demonstrate the tautology bypass on a vulnerable login, then fix it with parameterization and confirm the same input now fails safely.

lessons.title: XSS: Reflected, Stored & DOM
concepts: Cross-site scripting injects JavaScript into pages other users view: the attacker's script runs in the victim's browser, in the application's origin — reading session tokens, keylogging, or performing actions as the victim. The three types differ in delivery: reflected (payload in the request, e.g. a crafted link, executes immediately), stored (payload saved in the app — comments, profiles — executing for every viewer), and DOM-based (client-side JS unsafely handles attacker-controlled data).

Stored XSS is the most dangerous: one injection compromises every user who views the page, and it persists until someone finds and removes it. A stored XSS in a comment field plus an admin who reviews comments equals admin session theft. This is why output encoding matters everywhere user content is rendered — not just 'the obvious' fields.

The defenses, in order of effectiveness: context-aware output encoding (encode for the HTML, attribute, JS, or URL context you're in — encoding for the wrong context is no encoding), Content Security Policy (CSP headers that block inline scripts, neutering most payloads even if injected), and HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookie flags (so a successful XSS still can't easily steal the session token).

Testing mindset: every place the app reflects input — search boxes, error messages, usernames displayed on profiles — is a candidate. The minimal probe `` (or the subtler ``) tells you whether input is encoded. In your own apps, automate this: security scanners and CSP reporting catch what manual probing misses.

example.code:
Search results for:

Search results for:
example.walkthrough: The vulnerable template echoes the search query raw — the attacker's script executes in every visitor's browser and exfiltrates cookies to an external server. The fix encodes the output for the HTML context (neutralizing the tags) and adds a CSP header that blocks inline scripts entirely — defense in depth: even if an encoding is missed somewhere, the policy contains the blast radius.

pitfalls: Encoding once at input: stored data gets rendered in multiple contexts (HTML, JS, email) — encode at output, per context, every time.
CSP with 'unsafe-inline': the policy allows exactly what XSS needs — a strict script-src without inline scripts is what makes CSP effective.
Forgetting HttpOnly on session cookies: with it, document.cookie can't read the session token — without it, one XSS equals full session theft.
lessons.try_it: In a lab app, trigger a reflected XSS with a probe payload, then apply output encoding + CSP and confirm the same payload renders as inert text.

lessons.title: Authentication Attacks: Brute Force to Session Hijacking
concepts: Authentication is the most attacked surface of any app. The attack catalog: brute force (trying many passwords against one account), password spraying (trying few common passwords against many accounts — evades per-account lockout), credential stuffing (breached pairs, from the OSINT domain), and session hijacking (stealing the post-login token via XSS, sniffing, or fixation).

Defenses are layered: rate limiting and account lockout slow brute force (with careful lockout to avoid denial-of-service-by-lockout), MFA defeats password-only attacks entirely, breached-password screening blocks known-compromised choices, and generic error messages ('invalid credentials' for both bad-user and bad-password) deny enumeration oracles.

Session management is the second half: tokens must be long, random, and rotated at login (killing fixation), transmitted only over TLS with Secure flag, stored HttpOnly, and invalidated server-side on logout and password change. 'Logout' that only deletes the client-side cookie leaves the session valid for anyone holding it — test this in your own apps.

Password spraying deserves special attention because it defeats naive lockout: ten thousand accounts × three common passwords stays under every per-account threshold. Detection is behavioral — many accounts, few passwords, distributed sources — and the structural fix is MFA, which makes the correct password insufficient.

example.code:
# defensive auth checklist (implement all)
[ ] rate limit: 5 attempts/min/IP, exponential backoff
[ ] lockout: 10 fails -> 15 min (with CAPTCHA, not permanent)
[ ] MFA: required for all users, phishing-resistant preferred
[ ] breached-password screen at set/change time
[ ] generic errors: 'invalid username or password'
[ ] session: rotate at login, HttpOnly+Secure+SameSite,
      server-side invalidation on logout & password change
example.walkthrough: The checklist layers defenses so no single attack succeeds: rate limiting and lockout blunt brute force, MFA defeats password attacks structurally, breached-password screening blocks the stuffing ammunition, generic errors remove the enumeration oracle, and session hygiene (rotation, flags, server-side invalidation) protects the post-login state. Each line counters a specific attack from the catalog.

pitfalls: Permanent lockout after N failures: attackers lock out your users as a denial-of-service — use temporary lockout with CAPTCHA instead.
'Logout' that only clears the client cookie: the session stays valid server-side — always invalidate server-side.
MFA as optional: the accounts without it are the ones attackers find — require it, starting with privileged users.
lessons.try_it: Audit a lab app's login: test for enumeration (different errors?), test rate limiting (20 rapid attempts), and test whether logout invalidates the session server-side (replay the cookie).

lessons.title: SSRF & IDOR: Trusting User Input for Access Decisions
concepts: Server-Side Request Forgery: the app fetches a URL the user supplies (webhooks, image proxies, PDF generators, 'import from URL'). An attacker supplies `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` — the cloud metadata endpoint — and the server, which can reach it, returns IAM credentials. The server becomes the attacker's proxy into the internal network.

SSRF defenses: strict allowlists for fetchable hosts (not blocklists — attackers bypass those with DNS tricks, redirects, and decimal IP encodings), disable redirects or validate each hop, block cloud metadata IPs and RFC1918 ranges at the egress layer, and run fetchers in isolated network segments. The metadata endpoint specifically should require IMDSv2 (token-based) so even a successful SSRF gets nothing useful.

Insecure Direct Object Reference: the app exposes internal identifiers (`/invoice/12345`, `?user_id=842`) and trusts the client to only request their own. Changing the number accesses someone else's data. It's an authorization failure — authentication proved who you are, but nothing checked whether this object is yours.

IDOR fixes: indirect references (unguessable UUIDs instead of sequential IDs — defense in depth, not the fix), and the real fix — server-side authorization checks on every object access ('does the current user own invoice 12345?'). Test every object endpoint by swapping IDs between two test accounts; any cross-access is a finding.

example.walkthrough: The SSRF defense allowlists fetchable hosts (attackers defeat blocklists with encoding tricks; allowlists fail closed) and pairs it with egress firewall rules blocking metadata and private ranges. The IDOR defense is the authorization check: the invoice is loaded, then ownership is verified against the session user before any data renders — every object endpoint needs this, no exceptions.

pitfalls: SSRF blocklists: `169.254.169.254` blocked but `2852039166` (decimal) or a redirect not — allowlist hosts and block private ranges at egress.
Sequential IDs + 'security by obscurity': unguessable UUIDs slow attackers but the missing authz check is still the vulnerability — check ownership server-side.
IMDSv1 on cloud instances: SSRF to the metadata endpoint yields credentials — require IMDSv2 so token-less requests get nothing.
lessons.try_it: In a lab app, test two endpoints: one that fetches a user-supplied URL (try the metadata IP), one with a numeric object ID (swap IDs between two test users). Document both results.

lessons.title: Security Headers & WAF: The Outer Walls
concepts: HTTP security headers are cheap, high-value hardening: `Content-Security-Policy` (controls script sources — the XSS killer), `Strict-Transport-Security` (forces HTTPS, killing SSL-stripping), `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` (stops MIME-sniffing attacks), `X-Frame-Options`/`frame-ancestors` (clickjacking defense), and `Referrer-Policy` (controls data leakage via referers). `securityheaders.com` grades your deployment in seconds.

HSTS deserves emphasis: without it, a network attacker can strip HTTPS on first visit (sslstrip) — the user sees the site, the attacker sees everything. With `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains` (plus preload), the browser refuses plaintext — the downgrade attack dies. Deploy carefully: HSTS with broken HTTPS bricks your site until max-age expires.

A Web Application Firewall (ModSecurity, Cloudflare/AWS WAF) inspects HTTP traffic against attack signatures — blocking common SQLi/XSS payloads before they reach the app. It's valuable defense-in-depth: it buys time during zero-days and blocks automated attack noise. But it's not a fix — signature evasion is routine for targeted attackers, and a WAF never patches the underlying vulnerability.

The layered view: headers and WAF are the outer walls — they raise the cost of attack and catch the automated spray. The inner walls (parameterization, authz checks, encoding) are what stop a determined attacker. Assessments test both: run securityheaders.com against your apps, review WAF logs for what's being blocked, and fix the underlying code the WAF is compensating for.

example.walkthrough: Five headers, five attack classes neutralized: CSP contains XSS, HSTS kills protocol downgrade, nosniff stops MIME confusion, DENY stops clickjacking, and the referrer policy limits data leakage. The curl verification is the audit step — headers you assume are set but aren't are the most common finding in header reviews.

pitfalls: Deploying HSTS with broken HTTPS: browsers will refuse to connect until max-age expires — verify HTTPS fully first, then add HSTS with a short max-age and grow it.
WAF as the fix: the WAF blocks the signature while the vulnerability stays — treat WAF hits as bug reports for the underlying code.
CSP in report-only mode forever: report-only is for tuning, not protection — graduate to enforcing once the reports are clean.
lessons.try_it: Run securityheaders.com (or curl -sI) against a site you manage. Implement the missing headers, re-scan, and document the grade change.

lessons.title: Linux PrivEsc: SUID, Sudo & Capabilities
concepts: Privilege escalation turns a low-privilege foothold (web shell as www-data) into root. Linux offers three classic paths. SUID binaries run as their owner (often root): `find / -perm -4000` lists them, and any SUID binary with a shell escape, command execution, or writable path is a root shell waiting — GTFOBins catalogs which binaries are exploitable and how defenders should audit them.

Sudo misconfiguration is the most common real-world path: `sudo -l` shows what the user may run, and entries like `(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/vim` or `ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL` are game over — vim's `:!/bin/sh` is root. Even restricted commands fall: `sudo awk 'BEGIN {system("/bin/sh")}'`, wildcards in paths, and environment variable tricks. Audit sudoers with the attacker's eyes.

Capabilities are the modern, finer-grained SUID: `cap_setuid`, `cap_dac_override`, or `cap_sys_admin` on a binary grant root-like powers without full root. `getcap -r /` finds them. They're less audited than SUID — which is exactly why attackers love them — so add capability audits to your hardening checklist alongside the SUID scan.

The defensive triad: minimize (remove SUID from binaries that don't need it, scope sudo to exact commands with no wildcards), monitor (alert on SUID/capability changes — new SUID binaries are a persistence technique), and assume breach (an unprivileged foothold is one misconfiguration from root, so patch and audit continuously).

example.code:
# the attacker's enumeration (run defensively on your own hosts)
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null   # SUID binaries
sudo -l                                  # what can I run as whom?
getcap -r / 2>/dev/null                  # capabilities
# findings that are immediate escalations:
#  - SUID vim/nano/find/awk/perl/python -> GTFOBins shell escape
#  - (ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL -> total compromise
#  - cap_setuid on python3 -> root at will
example.walkthrough: The three enumeration commands are the attacker's first minute on a Linux foothold — and the defender's audit checklist. The findings list shows what 'vulnerable' looks like: SUID interpreters and editors are classic GTFOBins escapes, NOPASSWD ALL needs no technique at all, and capabilities on interpreters are SUID's stealthier cousin. Run these on your own fleet; every hit is a hardening ticket.

pitfalls: SUID-auditing once: package updates reintroduce SUID bits — audit continuously and alert on new SUID/capability appearances.
Sudo wildcards (`/usr/bin/*`): one entry covers every binary including shells — scope sudo to exact binaries with exact arguments.
Forgetting capabilities: the SUID scan is clean but `getcap` shows python3 with cap_setuid — audit both, always.
lessons.try_it: On your own Linux VM, run the three enumeration commands. For each SUID binary found, check GTFOBins: is it exploitable? Write the hardening action.

lessons.title: Credential Hunting: Files, History & Memory
concepts: Once on a box, attackers hunt credentials — and defenders must hunt the same way to find what shouldn't be there. The locations: shell history (`.bash_history` with `mysql -p'secret'`), config files (`.env`, `config.php`, `wp-config.php`), cloud metadata and instance profiles, CI/CD secret stores mounted into containers, and process memory (`/proc/<pid>/environ`, `gcore` dumps).

The methodology is grep-shaped: `grep -ri 'password' /etc /opt /home` (authorized, on your own systems), hunting for `AKIA`, `ghp_`, `xoxb-` patterns — the same patterns your gitleaks scans look for, but at runtime. Attackers automate this in seconds with tools like LinPEAS; defenders should run the same tools and remediate every hit.

Memory is the overlooked source: long-running processes hold secrets in RAM, and `/proc/<pid>/environ` exposes any process's environment to the same user. Core dumps from crashed services can contain credentials — which is why `ulimit -c 0` and dump-scrubbing matter. If the secret was ever in the process, assume memory forensics can recover it.

The structural fixes: secrets via vault/secret-manager injected at runtime (never in files or history), `HISTCONTROL=ignorespace` + no `-p'password'` invocations, least-privilege file permissions (config files 600, owned by the service user), and regular credential-hunting sweeps that treat every found secret as an incident — because to an attacker, it is one.

example.code:
# defensive credential hunt (your own systems, authorized)
grep -rIl --include='*.php' --include='*.env' -e 'password' -e 'secret' /srv/www 2>/dev/null
ls -la ~/.bash_history && grep -i 'pass\|token\|key' ~/.bash_history | head
# cloud: who can reach the metadata service?
curl -s http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ --max-time 3
# every hit below is a finding:
#  - password in .bash_history -> rotate + HISTCONTROL fix
#  - AKIA in /opt/app/config.yml -> rotate + move to secret manager
example.walkthrough: The hunt covers the three credential graveyards: config files grepped for secret patterns, shell history inspected for pasted passwords, and the cloud metadata endpoint probed for IAM credential exposure. Each hit maps to a concrete response — rotate the exposed secret, fix the mechanism that exposed it (history controls, secret manager), and treat the exposure window as an incident to investigate.

pitfalls: Hunting once: credentials accumulate with every deploy and debug session — sweep on a schedule, and gate deploys with secret scanning.
Finding secrets and just deleting them: the exposure window is unknown — rotate every found credential, then fix the source.
Storing the hunt results insecurely: a report listing every credential location is itself a treasure map — handle findings with the same care as the secrets.
lessons.try_it: On your own VM, run the hunt commands. For every credential found, write: where, what it accesses, rotation status, and the structural fix.

lessons.title: Persistence Mechanisms: How Attackers Stay (and How You Find Them)
concepts: Persistence is the attacker's answer to 'what if they reboot?' — mechanisms that re-establish access across restarts. On Linux: cron jobs (`/etc/cron.d/`, user crontabs), systemd services and timers, `.bashrc`/profile modifications, SSH authorized_keys additions, and malicious PAM modules. On Windows: Run keys, scheduled tasks, services, WMI subscriptions. Each is legitimate admin tooling repurposed.

The detection mindset is baselining: you can't spot the malicious cron job if you don't know the legitimate ones. Maintain known-good inventories of autostart locations, and alert on changes — new systemd service, new authorized_key, new scheduled task. Tools like OSQuery make this queryable: `SELECT * FROM crontab` across the fleet, diffed daily.

Authorized_keys is the classic: one appended public key gives persistent SSH access that survives password changes and most incident response ('we reset all passwords' doesn't remove the attacker's key). IR checklists must include authorized_keys, cron, and services review — password resets alone never evict a persistent attacker.

The advanced tier: kernel modules (rootkits hiding processes/files), bootkits, and firmware persistence — rare, but the reason high-value IR includes memory forensics and bare-metal rebuilds from known-good media. For most organizations, mastering the common mechanisms (cron, services, keys, tasks) covers the realistic threat.

example.code:
# Linux persistence audit (your own hosts)
ls -la /etc/cron.d/ /etc/cron.daily/ && for u in $(cut -f1 -d: /etc/passwd); do crontab -u $u -l 2>/dev/null; done
systemctl list-unit-files --type=service --state=enabled | grep -v '^ssh\|cron'
cat ~/.ssh/authorized_keys   # every key must map to a known person
ls /etc/systemd/system/*.timer
# Windows: schtasks /query, HKLM\...\Run, Get-ScheduledTask
example.walkthrough: The audit walks every common Linux persistence location: system and user crontabs, enabled systemd services (filtering the expected ones), SSH authorized keys (each must map to a real person), and systemd timers. Run this as a baseline on a clean host, then diff regularly — the new entry that wasn't there last week is the investigation.

pitfalls: Password-reset-only incident response: the attacker's cron job and authorized_key survive — IR must review persistence mechanisms explicitly.
No baseline: without known-good inventories, every audit is a guessing game — baseline clean hosts and alert on drift.
Ignoring user-level persistence: system cron is clean but the app user's crontab has the backdoor — audit all users, not just root.
lessons.try_it: On your lab VM, plant a test persistence mechanism (a cron job that logs), then run the audit and confirm you can find it. Then remove it and verify the audit is clean.

lessons.title: Living off the Land: LOLBins & LOLBAS
concepts: Living-off-the-land attacks use legitimate system tools as weapons: PowerShell, WMI, `certutil`, `bitsadmin` on Windows; `curl`, `python3`, `awk`, `find` on Linux. No malware to signature-detect — the tools are supposed to be there. LOLBAS (Living Off The Land Binaries And Scripts) catalogs Windows binaries and their abuse primitives; GTFOBins is the Linux equivalent.

The techniques: `certutil -urlcache -f` downloads files (a 'certificate utility' as a downloader), `bitsadmin` exfiltrates via background transfers, PowerShell's `IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString()` is the classic fileless payload, and WMI executes remotely without touching disk. Defenders can't block these tools — they're the OS — so detection must be behavioral.

Behavioral detection is the answer: Sysmon/EDR rules that flag `powershell -enc` (encoded commands), certutil with URL arguments, or `rundll32` with unusual DLLs. The parent-child process tree is the richest signal — `winword.exe` spawning `powershell.exe` is never legitimate, while `explorer.exe` spawning it might be. Baselining normal tool usage per role makes anomalies visible.

The hardening balance: constrain where possible (PowerShell Constrained Language Mode, AppLocker/WDAC allowlisting, disabling unused features), monitor everywhere else. Application allowlisting is the strongest control — if only approved binaries run, LOLBins outside the list die — but it requires the operational maturity to maintain the list.

example.code:
# detection: hunt LOLBin abuse in your own logs (Sysmon/EDR)
# parent-child anomalies:
#  winword.exe -> powershell.exe        ALWAYS investigate
#  certutil.exe with -urlcache -f       downloader abuse
#  powershell.exe -enc / -EncodedCommand encoded payload
#  rundll32.exe with network DLL        proxy execution
#
# hardening:
#  - PowerShell Constrained Language Mode via WDAC
#  - AppLocker/WDAC: allowlist approved binaries
#  - Sysmon config logging the above process creates
example.walkthrough: The hunt list names the specific command-line patterns that distinguish abuse from administration — encoded PowerShell, certutil downloads, anomalous parent-child trees. The hardening column shows the layered response: constrain the language mode, allowlist binaries, and log process creation so the behavior is visible. You can't remove these tools; you make their abuse visible and constrained.

pitfalls: Signature-only detection: LOLBin commands have no malware hash — behavioral rules on command lines and process trees are the detection.
Blocking PowerShell outright: breaks administration and pushes attackers to the next LOLBin — constrain and monitor instead.
Ignoring Linux LOLBins: `curl|bash`, python one-liners, and awk exfiltration are the Linux equivalents — the concept is cross-platform.
lessons.try_it: On your lab VM, run a benign LOLBin command (e.g., certutil download of a test file or python http.server) and check: does your logging capture the command line? If not, that's the gap.

lessons.title: Container Escape: From Container to Host
concepts: Containers share the host kernel — the isolation is namespaces and cgroups, not virtualization. Escape means breaking that containment: the classic paths are privileged containers (`--privileged` disables almost all isolation), mounted Docker sockets (`/var/run/docker.sock` in the container = root-equivalent on the host via the API), and host path mounts (`/:/host` then chroot).

The Docker socket is the crown jewel: any process that can talk to it can start a new privileged container with the host filesystem mounted — game over in one API call. `docker run -v /:/host -it alpine chroot /host` from inside a socket-mounted container gives a host root shell. This is why socket mounts are the first thing to grep for in any container audit.
