Kernel exploits are the no-misconfiguration path: a container running a vulnerable kernel version can exploit it to escape (Dirty COW, CVE-2022-0185 class). The defense is patching the host kernel — containers don't have their own kernels, so host patching protects every container at once. This is also why 'the container is patched' is meaningless for kernel CVEs.

Hardening checklist: never `--privileged` (use granular `--cap-add`), never mount the Docker socket (use sidecar patterns or socket proxies), mount host paths read-only and minimally, run as non-root with read-only filesystems, use seccomp/AppArmor profiles, and scan images. Kubernetes adds: PodSecurityStandards (restricted), no hostNetwork/hostPID, and admission control enforcing it all.

example.code:
# the socket-mount escape (lab only!)
# container started with: -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock
$ docker run -v /:/host --rm -it alpine chroot /host /bin/sh
# now you are root ON THE HOST - via the container
#
# audit for the misconfig:
$ docker inspect $(docker ps -q) | grep -A2 'docker.sock\|"Source": "/"'
# kubernetes: kubectl get pods -A -o yaml | grep -B2 -A2 'docker.sock\|hostPath'
example.walkthrough: The escape demonstrates the socket-mount catastrophe: from inside the container, the Docker API (via the mounted socket) launches a new container with the host's root filesystem mounted, and chroot makes it the new root — a host shell in one command. The audit commands show the defensive side: inspect every container for socket mounts and hostPath volumes, the two misconfigurations that make escape trivial.

pitfalls: Mounting the Docker socket 'for CI convenience': the CI job container gets host-root-equivalent — use socket proxies or the Docker-outside-of-Docker pattern with strict scoping.
--privileged 'to make it work': disables the isolation you deployed containers for — add only the specific capabilities needed.
Forgetting the host kernel: container image scans don't cover kernel CVEs — patch the host; it protects all containers at once.
lessons.try_it: In your lab, start a container with the Docker socket mounted, perform the escape, then remove the mount and confirm the escape path is dead. Write the audit check as a script.

lessons.title: Phishing Anatomy: Lures, Pretexts & Payloads
concepts: Phishing is the dominant initial-access vector because it attacks the human, not the firewall. Every phish has three parts: the lure (why you should act — urgency, authority, curiosity, fear), the pretext (the story that makes the request plausible — 'IT needs you to re-authenticate'), and the payload (the credential harvest, malicious attachment, or malicious link). Dissecting phish into these parts is how you train people to see through them.

The quality spectrum: commodity phish are bulk, typo-ridden, and caught by filters; spear phish target individuals with OSINT-derived details (your boss's name, your current project); whaling targets executives with high-value pretexts (fake acquisition documents, legal threats). The better the OSINT, the better the pretext — which is why the recon domain and this one are two halves of the same attack.

Payload evolution: credential harvesting via cloned login pages (Evilginx-style adversary-in-the-middle even defeats basic MFA by relaying the session), malicious Office macros and HTML smuggling, and QR-code phish ('quishing') that move the payload to the victim's phone — outside the corporate email filters. Defenses must track the payload, not just the email.

The defensive stack: technical (email authentication SPF/DKIM/DMARC, link rewriting, attachment sandboxing), procedural (out-of-band verification for sensitive requests — the 'call the requester back' rule), and human (simulated phishing with immediate, kind training on click — not punishment). No single layer holds; the stack does.

example.code:
Subject: Action Required: Password Expiry in 24h
From: IT-Support <it-support@examp1e.com>   <- look closely: '1' not 'l'
Body: 'Dear user, your password expires in 24 hours.
       Click here to keep your current password: http://bit.ly/3xK9mP'
--- dissection ---
lure:    urgency (24h) + authority (IT)
pretext: password expiry (plausible admin event)
payload:  credential harvest via shortened link
tells:    lookalike domain, generic greeting, URL shortener
example.walkthrough: The dissected phish shows all three parts: urgency plus authority as the lure, a plausible password-expiry story as the pretext, and a shortened link to a harvest page as the payload. The tells — lookalike domain, generic greeting, URL shortener — are what training teaches people to spot. This dissection format is exactly how you run a phishing-teardown exercise with a team.

pitfalls: Punishing clickers: shame makes people hide future clicks instead of reporting them — train immediately and kindly, celebrate reporters.
Testing with obviously fake phish: 'click here to win a yacht' teaches nothing — simulate with realistic pretexts built from actual OSINT.
Relying on the email filter alone: targeted phish bypass filters by design — the human layer must be trained as a sensor, not just a risk.
lessons.try_it: Take a real phish from your spam folder (or a public example). Dissect it into lure/pretext/payload and list three tells. Then write the 2-minute training version you'd give a colleague.

lessons.title: OSINT-Driven Pretexting
concepts: Pretexting is phishing's bespoke suit: instead of blasting a generic lure, the attacker builds a scenario from OSINT and plays a role inside it — the new IT hire following up on your laptop refresh, the auditor verifying badge access, the vendor confirming the invoice change. The pretext works because every verifiable detail checks out; only the request itself is malicious.

The OSINT-to-pretext pipeline: LinkedIn gives org charts and recent hires ('I just joined, Sarah in HR said to call you'); social media gives timing ('saw you were at the Austin conference — quick follow-up'); breach data gives the password-reset pretext; the company website gives the vendor names and the support portal URL to clone. Each public fact is a brick in a believable story.

Vishing (voice phishing) is pretexting's highest-conversion form: a confident caller with internal details bypasses skepticism that would stop an email. 'Hi, this is Mike from IT — we're pushing the VPN update tonight, I need you to approve the MFA prompt I'm about to send.' The MFA prompt arrives on cue (it's the attacker's login attempt), the victim approves, and the attacker is in — this defeats push-based MFA specifically.

Defense is procedural, not technical: the verification reflex ('let me call you back on the internal directory number'), MFA that resists relay (FIDO2/WebAuthn security keys — the prompt can't be forwarded), and a culture where verifying a colleague's identity is praised, not awkward. Run vishing simulations — the results will horrify you, which is the point.

example.code:
# the attacker's pretext worksheet (built from public OSINT)
Target:   helpdesk analyst (from LinkedIn 'open to work' post)
Role:      'Dave from infrastructure, following up on ticket #4821'
Details:   real ticket system name (from job posting),
            manager's name (LinkedIn), office move next month (press release)
Request:   'reset this VIP's password and read me the temp one'
Defense:   ticket-first policy + callback verification +
            no password readouts, ever (self-service reset links only)
example.walkthrough: The worksheet shows how public facts assemble into a pretext no helpdesk analyst would question — every detail is real except the caller's identity. The defense column is entirely procedural: tickets must exist before action, callbacks verify identity, and temp passwords are never read aloud. No technology detects this call; only process does.

pitfalls: Security questions as verification: mother's maiden name is OSINT — use non-public verifiers or, better, callback procedures.
Push-MFA as the last line: number matching helps, but FIDO2 keys are what actually defeat MFA-fatigue and relay attacks.
Making verification awkward: if employees fear offending by verifying, they won't — leadership must model and praise the callback.
lessons.try_it: Build a pretext worksheet for yourself from your own public OSINT (LinkedIn, social media). Then write the defensive procedure that would stop it.

lessons.title: Physical & Tailgating Basics
concepts: Physical access is total access: an attacker inside the building can plug into the network, plant devices, shoulder-surf, and walk out with assets. The attacks: tailgating (following an authorized person through the door — 'can you hold that? I'm carrying coffee'), badge cloning (RFID badges cloned with a $30 reader), and pretexted visits ('I'm here to service the printer').

The network-jack attack is the technical payload: plug a drop device (or a laptop) into an exposed Ethernet port in a lobby or conference room, and you're on the corporate LAN — often the same flat network as the servers. Rogue access points and planted keyloggers are the same idea: physical presence converted to persistent access.

Defenses are layered and human: badge-everyone policies with the cultural backing to challenge strangers ('I don't recognize you — can I help you find someone?' must be praise-worthy, not rude), 802.1X network authentication (so a plugged-in device gets nothing without credentials), disabled unused ports, and visitor escort policies that are actually enforced.

Red-team physical tests routinely succeed — which is why you should commission them: the findings ('we walked into the server room behind the pizza delivery') justify the 802.1X project and the badge-culture training far better than any slide deck. Physical security is tested by attempting it, not by asserting it.

example.code:
# physical assessment checklist (authorized test)
[ ] tailgate attempt at main entrance (with observer)
[ ] exposed network jacks in lobby/conference rooms?
[ ] 802.1X on wired ports? (plug in -> what happens?)
[ ] badge challenge culture: do employees question strangers?
[ ] server room: locked? who has access? logged?
[ ] clean desk: passwords on sticky notes? unlocked laptops?
example.walkthrough: The checklist turns physical security into testable claims: each line is an attempted action with an expected control. The network-jack test ('plug in — what happens?') is the technical core: with 802.1X the device gets nothing; without it, the tester is on the LAN. The badge-challenge line tests culture, which no technology replaces.

pitfalls: Assuming the badge reader is the security: tailgating bypasses it entirely — the control is the culture of challenging, plus 802.1X for the network.
Open network jacks 'for guests': every lobby port is a LAN invitation — disable unused ports, 802.1X the rest, give guests an isolated VLAN.
Never testing physically: the policy says 'challenge strangers' but nobody does — authorized tests reveal the gap before criminals do.
lessons.try_it: Walk your own office (or home office) with the checklist: exposed jacks, sticky-note passwords, unlocked screens, tailgating ease. Write three findings.

lessons.title: Building the Human Firewall
concepts: The human firewall is the trained workforce as a security sensor network: people who recognize attacks, report them fast, and verify instead of complying. Building it is a program, not a video: baseline phishing simulation, targeted training by role (finance gets BEC drills, helpdesk gets vishing drills), frictionless reporting (one-click phish button), and feedback loops (reporters hear what happened).

Metrics that matter: report rate (what fraction of simulated phish get reported — the real KPI), click rate trend (should fall), and time-to-report (fast reports let SOC kill the campaign). Click rate alone is vanity — a 2% click rate with 0% report rate means the 2% stay silent. Optimize for reporting, not just non-clicking.

The reporting pipeline must reward the behavior: every report gets acknowledged, true positives get thanks (publicly, with permission), and false positives get kind education ('good catch instinct — here's why this one was safe'). A reporter who feels foolish for a false positive never reports again — and the next real phish goes unreported.

Leadership modeling is the multiplier: when the CEO reports a phish and talks about it, reporting becomes culture. When executives demand exemptions from training, the program is theater. The human firewall is built top-down and measured bottom-up.

example.code:
# human firewall program (quarterly cadence)
baseline:   phish simulation -> click rate, report rate, time-to-report
train:      role-based modules (finance: BEC, helpdesk: vishing, devs: supply chain)
report:     one-click phish button in mail client; SOC triages in <15 min
feedback:   every reporter gets outcome ('you caught a real one!')
measure:    report rate trend is the KPI; review with leadership quarterly
example.walkthrough: The program cadence shows the closed loop: simulate to baseline, train by role (generic training doesn't stick), make reporting frictionless with fast SOC triage, close the loop with feedback to reporters, and measure the report-rate trend with leadership. Each element reinforces the others — training without reporting is knowledge without action; reporting without feedback dies.

pitfalls: Annual compliance video as 'training': click-through theater with zero behavior change — use frequent, role-relevant simulations with immediate coaching.
Punishing reporters of false positives: kills the reporting instinct — celebrate the vigilance, educate kindly on the miss.
Measuring only click rate: silent clickers are the danger — report rate and time-to-report are the KPIs that predict real incidents.
lessons.try_it: Draft a one-page human-firewall plan for a 50-person company: simulation frequency, role-based scenarios, reporting mechanism, and the three metrics you'd track.

lessons.title: Influence Principles: The Psychology Behind the Con
concepts: Robert Cialdini's six principles of influence explain why social engineering works — they're the same levers legitimate marketing uses. Reciprocity (the small gift — 'I got you this pen, now help me'), commitment/consistency ('you agreed to the security policy, right?'), social proof ('everyone in accounting already did this'), authority (the uniform, the title, the spoofed executive), liking (friendliness, similarity, compliments), and scarcity ('this offer expires today').

Attackers weaponize them deliberately: the vishing caller opens with liking (friendly, uses your name, mentions your team), establishes authority ('I'm with the security team'), creates scarcity/urgency ('the system locks in 10 minutes'), and invokes social proof ('your colleagues already verified'). Recognizing the pattern in real time is the defense — name the principle, break the spell.

Each principle has a counter-procedure, not just awareness: authority → verify identity out-of-band (the principle can't survive a callback); scarcity/urgency → the mandatory pause ('urgent requests get verified, that's the policy'); social proof → 'show me the ticket' (claims about others are checkable); reciprocity → separate the gift from the request ('thanks, but I still need verification').

Training with the principles beats training with examples: examples go stale (yesterday's phish template), but the six principles are stable — every new AI-enhanced lure still runs on authority + urgency + liking. Teach people to spot the lever being pulled, and they generalize to attacks that haven't been invented yet.

example.code:
# spotting the levers (real vishing transcript, annotated)
Caller: 'Hi Sarah! It's Mike from IT security [LIKING: name, friendly].'
Caller: 'We're doing the mandatory verification [AUTHORITY: 'mandatory'].
         Your whole floor already completed it [SOCIAL PROOF].'
Caller: 'I need it in the next 5 minutes or your account locks [SCARCITY].'
Sarah:  'Okay... what's the ticket number? [COUNTER: verify, don't comply]'
Caller:  *hangs up*   # the procedure beat the psychology
example.walkthrough: The annotated transcript shows four influence levers deployed in 30 seconds — liking, authority, social proof, scarcity — and the single counter that defeats all of them: the verification procedure ('what's the ticket number?'). The attacker hangs up because the procedure doesn't run on psychology. This is the training artifact: teach the levers, drill the counter.

pitfalls: Training on examples only: 'watch for the gift-card phish' — attackers change the example weekly; the principles are the stable defense.
Awareness without procedure: knowing about authority bias doesn't stop compliance under pressure — the counter must be a practiced reflex (the callback, the ticket check).
Assuming smart people are immune: intelligence doesn't protect against influence principles — process does; everyone verifies, no exceptions.
lessons.try_it: Take a phish from your spam folder and label every influence principle it uses. Then write the one-line counter-procedure for each principle.

lessons.title: The IR Lifecycle: Prepare to Lessons Learned
concepts: Incident response follows the NIST lifecycle: Preparation (the only phase you control before the incident — playbooks, tooling, contact lists, backups), Detection & Analysis (is this real? what's the scope?), Containment (stop the bleeding), Eradication (remove the cause), Recovery (restore service safely), and Lessons Learned (the postmortem that prevents recurrence).

Preparation is where incidents are won: an IR retainer or internal team identified, playbooks for the likely scenarios (ransomware, BEC, data exposure), log sources centralized with adequate retention (you can't investigate what you didn't log), and backups tested — 'we have backups' untested is a hope, not a control. Tabletop exercises turn the playbook from a document into muscle memory.

Severity classification drives everything: SEV-1 (active breach/data loss — all hands, executive comms), SEV-2 (contained but serious), SEV-3 (suspicious, investigating). The classification decides who gets woken, what comms go out, and whether legal gets involved. Deciding this during the incident wastes the golden hour — classify from a matrix, not from debate.

The two questions that govern the whole lifecycle: 'what's the scope?' (which systems, which data, still active?) and 'is it contained?' Every action — from pulling plugs to calling legal — flows from the answers. IR is scope management under time pressure, and the lifecycle is the checklist that keeps panic from skipping steps.

example.code:
# IR lifecycle at a glance (NIST SP 800-61)
1. PREPARATION   playbooks, logging, backups, tabletops, retainer
2. DETECTION     alert -> triage: real? scope? severity?
3. CONTAINMENT   isolate hosts, block C2, preserve evidence
4. ERADICATION   remove malware, close vuln, rotate creds
5. RECOVERY      restore from clean backups, monitor hard
6. LESSONS       postmortem -> action items -> playbook updates
# golden rule: scope before action; evidence before eradication
example.walkthrough: The lifecycle is a checklist against panic: each phase has a clear exit criterion, and the golden rule at the bottom orders the instincts — understand scope before acting (or you'll contain the wrong things), and preserve evidence before eradicating (or you'll destroy the investigation). Preparation is listed first because it's the only phase that happens before the 2 AM call.

pitfalls: Skipping preparation: no playbook, no logs, no tested backups — the incident is then improvised, which is how 2-hour outages become 2-week ones.
Eradicating before scoping: wiping the malware before understanding the foothold means the attacker walks back in through the same door tomorrow.
No lessons-learned phase: the same incident recurs next quarter — the postmortem is what converts cost into prevention.
lessons.try_it: Draft a one-page IR playbook for ransomware at a 50-person company: severity matrix, first-30-minutes checklist, contact list roles, and comms templates.

lessons.title: Triage: Scoping a Compromise
concepts: Triage answers three questions fast: Is it real? (true positive vs misconfigured alert), What's the scope? (which hosts, accounts, data — and is the attacker still active?), and How bad? (severity classification). Speed matters, but wrong-fast is worse than right-slow: mis-scoping sends the response at the wrong target.

The scoping toolkit: EDR telemetry (process trees on flagged hosts), authentication logs (which accounts touched which systems when), network flows (who talked to the C2, what exfiltrated), and email logs (who else got the phish). Correlate across sources — the EDR alert is one host; the auth logs reveal the other nine.

The 'patient zero plus N' method: from the initial indicator, expand along each axis — lateral movement (which hosts did this account touch?), credential spread (which accounts logged into the compromised host?), data access (what did they read?), and time (when did it start? — assume earlier than the first alert). Document the scope as you go; it changes.

Communicate the working scope explicitly and timestamp it: 'As of 09:40, scope is 3 hosts, 1 account, no evidence of data exfiltration — investigating lateral movement.' Stale scope kills: teams act on yesterday's 'just one host' while the attacker owns twelve. Re-scope on a cadence until contained.

example.code:
# triage expansion (from one EDR alert)
patient zero: WS-0427 (mimikatz-like behavior, 08:12)
  -> auth logs: svc-backup logged into WS-0427, SRV-FILE-02, SRV-DB-01
  -> expand: EDR on all three; SRV-DB-01 shows lateral tooling
  -> email: same user got phish 07:58, clicked 08:03
  -> scope v1 (09:40): 3 hosts, 1 svc account, phish vector confirmed
  -> action: isolate all three, rotate svc-backup creds, hunt phish recipients
example.walkthrough: The triage walk shows expansion along each axis from a single EDR alert: auth logs reveal the service account's lateral movement, EDR confirms tooling on the new hosts, email logs identify the phish vector. The scope statement is versioned and timestamped — v1 at 09:40 — because scope is a living assessment, and the actions (isolate, rotate, hunt) flow directly from it.

pitfalls: Trusting the first alert as the whole scope: the EDR flagged one host; the auth logs showed three — triage expands, never assumes.
Scope without timestamps: 'three hosts' from yesterday's briefing misleads today's response — version and timestamp every scope statement.
Analysis paralysis: perfect scope takes days; work the 80% scope now (isolate, rotate) while refining — triage is time-boxed.
lessons.try_it: Given a simulated alert (pick any from this bootcamp's scenarios), write the triage expansion: the three questions, the log sources you'd check, and a v1 scope statement.

lessons.title: Containment Strategies
concepts: Containment stops the bleeding without destroying the evidence: isolate hosts (EDR network quarantine — host stays on for forensics, talks to nothing), block C2 domains/IPs at the perimeter, disable compromised accounts (not delete — deletion destroys the audit trail), and revoke sessions and tokens. Each action buys time while preserving the investigation.

Short-term vs long-term containment: short-term is the tourniquet (isolate now, ask later — applied in minutes), long-term is the fix that lets you restore service (rebuild the vulnerable service, rotate the credential class, deploy the missing control). Confusing the two means either acting too slowly ('let's plan the perfect response') or restoring too early ('we isolated it, turn everything back on').

The evidence-preservation tension: wiping and rebuilding is the fastest eradication, but it destroys forensic evidence — and if you haven't found the persistence mechanism, the rebuilt host gets recompromised. Order of operations: image/collect first (memory, disk), then eradicate. The business pressure to 'just get it back online' is the enemy of this ordering — the IR lead must hold the line.

Ransomware-specific containment: disconnect (but don't power off — memory holds keys and evidence), identify the variant (ID Ransomware service), check for decryptors before considering payment, and assume the backups are targeted — verify offline/air-gapped copies before trusting any restore. Never pay without exhausting recovery options and involving legal.

example.code:
# containment runbook (first 30 minutes)
[ ] EDR-isolate affected hosts (network quarantine, host stays up)
[ ] block C2 indicators at firewall/proxy (from threat intel)
[ ] disable (not delete) compromised accounts; revoke sessions
[ ] snapshot memory + disk images BEFORE any wiping
[ ] identify ransomware variant (if any); check decryptor availability
[ ] comms: notify IR lead, legal, exec per severity matrix
example.walkthrough: The runbook orders the golden hour: isolate and block (stop the bleeding), disable accounts without deleting (preserve audit trails), image everything before any wipe (evidence first), then the ransomware-specific checks. Each line is a 5-minute action — the whole list is the first 30 minutes, executable under pressure because the decisions were made during preparation.

pitfalls: Deleting compromised accounts: destroys the audit trail the investigation needs — disable, preserve, investigate.
Wiping before imaging: fastest recovery, zero evidence, and the persistence mechanism you didn't find recompromises the rebuild — image first.
Restoring from the 'backups' without verifying: ransomware targets backups first — verify offline/air-gapped copies or you'll restore the encryption.
lessons.try_it: Tabletop this runbook with a colleague: one plays IR lead, one plays the business owner demanding systems back online. Practice holding the evidence-first ordering under pressure.

lessons.title: Eradication & Recovery
concepts: Eradication removes the cause: kill the malware, delete persistence mechanisms (the cron jobs, services, keys from the persistence domain), close the exploited vulnerability (patch, config fix), and rotate every credential the attacker could have touched — which, for a domain compromise, means the krbtgt account twice (to invalidate all Kerberos tickets) and every service account.

The 'could have touched' standard is deliberately broad: you don't rotate what you proved compromised, you rotate what was reachable. Attackers don't leave receipts for everything they read. Under-rotation is how 'eradicated' incidents recur — the attacker kept one API key you deemed 'probably fine.'

Recovery restores service in priority order: rebuild from known-good media (not 'cleaned' systems — rootkits lie; nuke from orbit), restore data from verified clean backups, and bring systems online in phases with enhanced monitoring. The enhanced monitoring period (2-4 weeks of heightened alerting) catches the persistence you missed — assume you missed something.

The recovery trap is speed pressure: the business wants everything back today, but phased recovery with monitoring is what prevents the second incident. Define the recovery order in the playbook (critical revenue systems first), get executive sign-off on the timeline during preparation, and don't let the 2 AM pressure renegotiate it.

example.code:
# eradication checklist (before any recovery)
[ ] persistence mechanisms removed (cron, services, keys, tasks)
[ ] exploited vuln patched / misconfig fixed (root cause!)
[ ] credentials rotated: user accounts, service accounts,
      API keys, krbtgt twice (domain compromise)
[ ] malware removed / hosts rebuilt from known-good media
# recovery (phased, monitored)
[ ] restore data from VERIFIED clean backups
[ ] bring up in priority order; enhanced monitoring 2-4 weeks
[ ] validate: no re-compromise indicators during watch period
example.walkthrough: The checklist enforces the ordering: eradication is complete (persistence gone, root cause fixed, credentials rotated to the 'could have touched' standard, hosts rebuilt — not cleaned) before recovery begins. Recovery is phased with a 2-4 week enhanced-monitoring tail, because the honest assumption is that something was missed, and the monitoring is designed to catch it.

pitfalls: 'Cleaning' compromised hosts: rootkits and firmware persistence survive cleaning — rebuild from known-good media for anything the attacker touched with privilege.
Rotating only proven-compromised credentials: attackers don't itemize — rotate everything reachable, including krbtgt twice for domain incidents.
Declaring victory at restore: the enhanced-monitoring period is part of recovery, not optional — most recurrences surface in the first two weeks.
lessons.try_it: Write an eradication checklist for a simulated web-shell incident: persistence locations to clear, credentials to rotate, and the rebuild-vs-clean decision per host.

lessons.title: SSH Hardening Beyond Defaults
concepts: OpenSSH's defaults favor compatibility over security: password authentication enabled, root login permitted (prohibit-password on some distros), and no rate limiting. Hardening starts in `sshd_config`: `PasswordAuthentication no` (keys only), `PermitRootLogin no` (no direct root — use sudo with full auditing), `MaxAuthTries 3`, and `AllowUsers`/`AllowGroups` to whitelist who may connect at all.

Key management is the other half: `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` entries should use `from=` restrictions and `command=` forced commands where appropriate; stale keys (the 'ghost keys' scenario) must be pruned on offboarding — automate it, because manual processes miss. Ed25519 keys are the modern default: faster and smaller than RSA with equivalent security.

Fail2ban (or sshd's own rate limiting) blunts brute force, but the structural fix for internet-facing SSH is removing it from the internet: VPN/bastion-only access, port knocking for the exotic, or Tailscale-style mesh. Every SSH port on 0.0.0.0 is a standing invitation to the world's botnets — Shodan will list it within hours.

Verify hardening with `sshd -T` (dumps effective configuration — what sshd actually uses, not what you think you wrote) and an external port scan. Configuration that isn't verified is a hope: the number of 'hardened' servers still allowing password auth is a perennial audit finding.

example.code:
# /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/hardening.conf
PasswordAuthentication no
PermitRootLogin no
MaxAuthTries 3
AllowGroups ssh-users
X11Forwarding no
# verify effective config:
$ sshd -T | grep -Ei 'passwordauth|permitroot|maxauthtries'
passwordauthentication no
permitrootlogin no
maxauthtries 3
example.walkthrough: The hardening snippet disables password auth and root login, caps auth tries, and whitelists the ssh-users group — X11 forwarding off as hygiene. The `sshd -T` verification is the critical step: it prints the effective configuration after all includes and defaults, proving the hardening is actually active rather than assumed.

pitfalls: Editing sshd_config without `sshd -T` verification: includes and defaults can override your intent — always verify effective config.
Allowing password auth 'for emergencies': the emergency becomes the attacker's entry — keys plus a break-glass procedure instead.
Forgetting AllowUsers/AllowGroups: every account on the box becomes an SSH target — whitelist explicitly.
lessons.try_it: Harden SSH on your lab VM with the snippet, verify with `sshd -T`, then confirm password login fails and key login works.

lessons.title: Filesystem Hardening: Mount Options & Permissions
concepts: The filesystem is the battleground for persistence and privesc: mount options are your first controls. `nodev` (no device files), `nosuid` (SUID bits ignored), and `noexec` (no binaries executed) on `/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, and removable media neuter entire attack classes — the classic `/tmp` SUID-drop dies at the mount level. `/etc/fstab` makes it permanent; `findmnt` verifies it.

Permissions hygiene: world-writable files (`-perm -0002`) are attacker conveniences — find and fix them; sensitive files (keys, configs) should be 600 owned by the service user; and the sticky bit on `/tmp` (1777) prevents users deleting each other's files. `find / -xdev -perm -4000` (SUID) and `-perm -0002` (world-writable) are the recurring audit pair.

Immutable flags (`chattr +i`) protect critical files (resolv.conf, hosts, authorized_keys for service accounts) from modification even by root — until the flag is removed. It's a speed bump against automated malware, not a vault, but speed bumps compose: the attacker fighting immutables, nosuid mounts, and read-only roots is having a bad day.

Read-only root filesystems (with tmpfs for the writable bits) are the endgame for appliances and containers: the attacker can't persist to disk at all. Combined with verified boot, the host becomes disposable — compromise it and you reimage, because there's nothing to salvage and nowhere to hide.

example.code:
$ findmnt -o TARGET,OPTIONS /tmp
TARGET OPTIONS
/tmp   rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,relatime
$ find / -xdev \( -perm -4000 -o -perm -0002 \) -type f 2>/dev/null
/usr/bin/sudo
/tmp/evil-drop      # <- world-writable in /tmp: investigate!
$ chattr +i /etc/resolv.conf   # even root can't modify until -i
example.walkthrough: The mount options show /tmp properly neutered — no SUID, no devices, no execution. The find command surfaces both the legitimate (sudo) and the suspicious (a world-writable file in /tmp) in one pass. The immutable flag on resolv.conf demonstrates the extra layer: even a root compromise must first remove the flag, which is itself an auditable event.

pitfalls: noexec on /tmp breaking legitimate installers: some apps execute from /tmp — use a dedicated exec-allowed scratch dir instead of weakening /tmp.
Setting +i and forgetting: updates fail mysteriously months later — document immutables or the next admin 'fixes' them away.
Auditing permissions once: packages and admins change things — schedule the SUID/world-writable scan, alert on new entries.
lessons.try_it: Apply nosuid/nodev/noexec to /tmp on your lab VM via /etc/fstab, then verify a SUID binary copied there no longer escalates.

lessons.title: Auditd & System Logging
concepts: You can't investigate what you didn't log: auditd is Linux's kernel-level auditing — it records syscalls (file access, execs, privilege changes) per your rules. The essential ruleset: watch `/etc/passwd`, `/etc/shadow`, `/etc/sudoers` for writes; log all `execve` of suspicious binaries; track `chmod`/`chown` on sensitive paths. Without this, 'who changed sudoers?' is unanswerable.

Centralize everything: rsyslog/journald forwarding to a hardened log server (that attackers can't reach to delete), with integrity protections. Local logs are the attacker's first deletion target — `rm /var/log/auth.log` is incident-response 101 for them. Logs that exist only on the compromised host are already compromised.

Log volume vs value: auditd can generate enormous output — tune rules to the meaningful (writes to sensitive files, privilege escalations, new binaries executed) rather than everything. The SIEM/useful-logging discipline: every rule should map to a detection ('SUID bit set on new binary → alert'), or it's noise that hides the signal.

Retention and integrity: size log storage for your retention target (90 days minimum for serious IR), sign or hash log batches, and alert on logging gaps — an attacker who stops the logging service creates a silence that is itself the loudest alert. Monitor the monitors.

example.code:
# /etc/audit/rules.d/hardening.rules
-w /etc/passwd -p wa -k identity
-w /etc/shadow -p wa -k identity
-w /etc/sudoers -p wa -k priv_esc
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S execve -k executions
# forward to central log host:
# /etc/rsyslog.d/forward.conf: *.* @@loghost.example.com:514
$ ausearch -k priv_esc --start recent | head
example.walkthrough: The audit rules watch identity files and sudoers for writes/attribute changes, and log every program execution on 64-bit — the raw material for 'who ran what, when.' Rsyslog forwards everything to the central host so local deletion doesn't blind you. The ausearch query demonstrates the payoff: filter by key and time to answer 'who touched privilege config recently?' in seconds.

pitfalls: Logging locally only: the attacker's first move is deleting local logs — forward to an unreachable-by-attackers central host.
Audit-everything rules: terabytes of noise that nobody reads — tune to detections, alert on the meaningful, archive the rest.
No alerting on logging gaps: a stopped auditd is the attacker's invisibility cloak — monitor the logging pipeline itself.
lessons.try_it: Deploy the ruleset on your lab VM, trigger a sudoers touch, and find it with ausearch. Then stop auditd and confirm your (simulated) monitor notices.

lessons.title: iptables/nftables Rule Design
concepts: Linux firewalls are default-deny systems wearing default-allow clothes: the professional posture is deny-by-default with explicit allows. The rule order matters — iptables/nftables evaluate top-down, first match wins — so the structure is: allow established/related (return traffic), allow loopback, allow the specific services, log-and-drop the rest. One misplaced rule above the allows punches the hole.

The stateful core: `-m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT` as the first rule lets return traffic through without opening inbound ports. This single rule is what makes 'allow outbound, deny inbound' work — without it, you'd have to open inbound ports for every outbound connection's replies.

nftables is the modern successor (single framework replacing iptables/ip6tables/arptables/ebtables): `nft add rule inet filter input tcp dport 22 accept` with sets for efficient IP lists. New deployments should use nftables; the concepts (chains, tables, stateful matching) transfer directly from iptables knowledge.

The verification discipline: `iptables -L -n -v --line-numbers` (or `nft list ruleset`) to read what's actually loaded, plus an external scan to confirm the intended exposure. Firewall rules that aren't verified are the 'we thought port 22 was restricted' incident — and test from outside, because local rules don't show you the cloud security group above them.

example.walkthrough: The nftables ruleset implements default-deny with explicit allows: established connections first (return traffic), loopback, then exactly three service ports — everything else hits the drop policy after being logged. The log prefix gives you the dropped-packet telemetry for tuning. Verification is two-sided: read the loaded ruleset, then scan from outside to confirm reality matches intent.

pitfalls: Allow rules above the established rule: return traffic gets dropped and 'the firewall broke the app' — established/related goes first, always.
Forgetting ip6tables/nft inet family: IPv4 locked down, IPv6 wide open — the dual-stack hole; nftables' inet family covers both by design.
No external verification: the local rules look right but the cloud security group allows 0.0.0.0 — test from outside the host.
lessons.try_it: Write the nftables (or iptables) ruleset on your lab VM, load it, then scan from another host and confirm only the intended ports are open.

lessons.title: TLS Interception & Certificate Pinning
concepts: TLS interception (corporate proxies decrypting traffic for inspection) breaks the end-to-end guarantee: the proxy presents its own certificate, and clients must trust the proxy's CA. The security tradeoff is real — inspection catches malware and data theft, but the proxy becomes a high-value target holding everyone's plaintext, and a compromised proxy CA means undetectable interception.

Certificate pinning is the countermeasure for high-value apps: the app ships with the expected certificate/SPKI hash and refuses connections presenting anything else — including the corporate proxy's cert. Mobile banking apps pin; that's why they 'don't work on corporate wifi.' Pinning trades inspection-compatibility for interception-resistance.

The operational hazards of pinning: certificate rotation bricks the app if the pin isn't updated (pin the CA or a backup pin, not just the leaf), and debugging becomes harder. HPKP (HTTP pinning) died from exactly these footguns — modern pinning lives in app code (mobile) or DANE/CAA (DNS-based), not in HTTP headers.

For defenders: know where interception happens in your environment (it affects what 'encrypted' means for DLP and forensics), ensure the proxy CA is properly deployed and the proxy itself is hardened and monitored, and exempt (or specially handle) pinned apps rather than breaking them silently.

example.code:
# check what the client actually sees (is there a proxy?)
$ openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com 2>/dev/null | \
    openssl x509 -noout -issuer -subject
issuer=C = US, O = Corporate Proxy CA    # <- interception!
subject=CN = example.com
# vs direct:
issuer=C = US, O = Let's Encrypt
example.walkthrough: The openssl check reveals interception: the issuer is the corporate proxy CA, not the site's real CA (Let's Encrypt). The subject is still example.com — the proxy faithfully impersonates the site. This is how you audit whether your traffic is being intercepted: compare the presented issuer against the expected CA. On a network without interception, the issuer would be the public CA.

pitfalls: Pinning the leaf certificate only: rotation day bricks every client — pin the CA/SPKI with backup pins and a rotation plan.
Ignoring proxy CA deployment: half the fleet doesn't trust the proxy CA, so users click through warnings — training them to ignore the exact warnings that matter.
Assuming 'HTTPS' means end-to-end: on intercepting networks it means client-to-proxy — know your environment's reality for forensics and DLP.
lessons.try_it: Run the openssl issuer check on your network vs a mobile hotspot. Document whether interception is present and which CA performs it.

lessons.title: Network Segmentation & VLANs
concepts: Flat networks are attacker playgrounds: one compromised host can reach everything — workstations, servers, IoT cameras, the printer with the default password. Segmentation divides the network into zones (VLANs + firewall rules between them) so a breach in one zone doesn't mean breach of all: user VLAN can't reach server VLAN except on required ports; IoT VLAN can't reach anything but the internet.

The zone model: outside (internet), DMZ (public-facing servers), internal user segments, server segments, management network (the most restricted — admin interfaces live here, reachable only via bastion/VPN), and IoT/quarantine. Firewall rules between zones default-deny; each allow is a documented business need. The management network isolation is what stops 'compromised workstation → admin interface' pivots.

VLAN hopping is the attack to know: double-tagging (sending frames with two VLAN tags to hop from native VLAN) and switch spoofing (tricking the switch into trunking). Defenses: never use VLAN 1, set native VLAN to unused, disable auto-trunking (DTP off), and treat VLANs as a segmentation aid — not a security boundary by themselves. Real boundaries are firewall rules between zones.

Microsegmentation (host firewalls, zero-trtrust overlays) extends this to the workload level: each server's iptables only accepts its required peers. The flat-network incident you'll read about next quarter will be another reminder — segment now, or scope the breach later.

example.code:
# zone firewall intent (example)
# users -> servers: 443 only (app), 22 DENY
# servers -> internet: 443 for updates, DENY all else
# iot -> *: DENY all except DHCP/DNS to gateway
# mgmt: reachable ONLY via bastion host (VPN)
# inter-VLAN routing: firewall, not the L3 switch alone
$ # verify: from a user-VLAN host, attempt ssh to server VLAN -> must fail
example.walkthrough: The intent list shows zone thinking: each arrow is a policy, default-deny, with the management network reachable only through the bastion. The verification line is the audit: from the user zone, the SSH attempt to the server zone must fail — segmentation you don't test is segmentation you don't have. Firewalling the inter-VLAN routing (not just switching it) is what makes the zones real.

pitfalls: VLANs without inter-zone firewalling: traffic routes freely between VLANs — you've labeled the flat network, not segmented it.
Native VLAN 1 everywhere: double-tagging attacks hop VLANs — use an unused native VLAN and disable DTP.
Management interfaces on the user LAN: the compromised workstation pivots straight to the admin panel — isolate management behind bastion/VPN.
lessons.try_it: Draw your home/lab network as zones, write the inter-zone policy list, and test one deny rule (e.g., block a port between two lab VMs).

lessons.title: Bash Safety: set -euo pipefail
concepts: Bash's defaults are footguns: a failed command doesn't stop the script (it continues into the wreckage), unset variables expand to empty strings (so `rm -rf $DIR/` with unset DIR becomes `rm -rf /`), and pipeline failures are masked (the exit status is the last command's — `false | true` 'succeeds'). `set -euo pipefail` fixes all three: exit on error, error on unset variables, and pipelines fail if any stage fails.

`set -e` (errexit): the script dies on the first failing command — no more 'the download failed but we deployed the empty directory anyway.' Caveat: it doesn't trigger inside `if` conditions or `||` fallbacks (by design), and it can't save you from `grep` returning 1 on no-match — handle expected non-zero exits explicitly.

`set -u` (nounset): referencing an unset variable is a fatal error — the `$DIR/` catastrophe becomes a loud failure instead of a deleted root. Pair with `${VAR:-default}` for intentional defaults. `set -o pipefail`: the pipeline's status is the rightmost non-zero exit — `mysqldump | gzip > backup.sql.gz` now actually tells you when the dump failed instead of archiving the error message.

The shebang line `#!/usr/bin/env bash` plus `set -euo pipefail` as lines 1-2 is the professional baseline — and ShellCheck (the linter) catches the rest: unquoted variables, `cd` without checks, `rm -rf` with variables. CI should shellcheck every script; the rm -rf incident in this bootcamp's scenarios is what happens without it.

example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
BACKUP_DIR="${1:?usage: backup.sh <dir>}"   # :? errors if unset/empty
cd "$BACKUP_DIR" || exit 1
tar czf backup.tgz . | tee backup.log
# without pipefail: tar fails, tee succeeds, script reports SUCCESS
# without -u: empty $1 -> BACKUP_DIR empty -> tar of '.' ...
# without -e: failed cd continues, tars the wrong directory
example.walkthrough: The script's first two lines are the safety baseline. `${1:?...}` fails loudly on missing arguments instead of operating on an empty path. The comments show each flag's kill: pipefail catches the tar failure the tee would mask, -u catches the empty argument, -e stops the script when cd fails rather than archiving the wrong directory. Every line defends against a real incident class.

pitfalls: set -e with `grep` in pipelines: grep exits 1 on no match — expected non-zero becomes fatal; handle with `|| true` where no-match is fine.
Unquoted variables (`rm -rf $DIR`): word splitting and globbing turn paths into multiple arguments — quote every expansion, always.
`cd` without `|| exit`: the cd fails, the script continues in the wrong directory — check every cd or use `set -e` (and still check).
lessons.try_it: Take an old script of yours (or write one) and add `set -euo pipefail` + ShellCheck. Fix every warning; note which ones were real bugs.

lessons.title: Python for Security Automation
concepts: Python is the security automator's language: readable, with libraries for everything — `requests` for HTTP, `scapy` for packets, `paramiko` for SSH, `python-nmap` wrapping scans, and `argparse` for CLIs your team will actually use. Bash glues commands; Python builds tools. The crossover point is about 50 lines or any structured data — that's when bash becomes write-only.

The automation patterns: log parsing (read once, extract indicators, output CSV/JSON for the SIEM), API glue (pull Shodan/HIBP/VirusTotal data on a schedule), and response actions (isolate the host via EDR API when the detector fires). Each script should be idempotent, logged, and exit-coded — automation that can't be re-run safely is a liability.

Subprocess safety: `subprocess.run([...], capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=30)` with argument lists (never `shell=True` with formatted strings — that's command injection in your own tooling). Timeouts on every external call; a hung subprocess at 3 AM is how your response script becomes part of the incident.

Error handling for security tools: distinguish 'target unreachable' from 'tool broken' from 'finding: vulnerable' — three different exit paths, three different alerts. A scanner that reports 'all clear' when it crashed is worse than no scanner. Test the failure modes, not just the happy path.

example.walkthrough: The script demonstrates the automation pattern: clear purpose in the docstring, structured exit codes (2 = finding, 0 = clean), timeouts on every connection, and resource cleanup in finally. It's re-runnable, its output is machine-parseable, and a crash looks different from a finding — the three properties that separate a tool from a script.

pitfalls: shell=True with f-strings: your automation tooling gets command injection — always argument lists, never shell strings.
No timeouts on network calls: one hung host hangs the whole 3 AM scan — timeout everything external.
'All clear' on crash: unhandled exceptions should exit non-zero and alert — a scanner that fails silent is a blind spot.
lessons.try_it: Write a Python script that parses an auth log, counts failed logins per IP, and exits 2 if any IP exceeds a threshold. Make it idempotent and timeout-safe.

lessons.title: Parsing Logs with awk, sed & jq
concepts: Most security data lives in logs, and the command-line trio is the fastest way to interrogate them. `awk` is a column processor: `awk '{print $1}'` extracts fields, `awk '$9==404'` filters rows — the access log becomes a queryable table. `sed` is the stream editor for substitution and extraction. `jq` does for JSON logs what awk does for text — and modern infrastructure logs JSON.

The access-log interrogation pattern: top talkers (`awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head`), error hunters (`awk '$9 >= 400'`), and attack signatures (`grep -c 'wp-login'`, `grep 'union.*select' -i`). These one-liners are the first 5 minutes of any web incident — before the SIEM, before the ticket.

jq for JSON logs: `jq 'select(.status>=500)' app.json`, `jq -r '[.ip, .path] | @tsv'`, `jq -s 'group_by(.ip) | map({ip: .[0].ip, n: length}) | sort_by(.n) | reverse | .[0:10]'` for top offenders. Cloud and container logs are JSON — jq fluency is non-optional for modern IR.

Pipeline discipline: build incrementally (each pipe stage verified before adding the next), mind the memory (sort on huge files needs disk), and save the pipeline as a script when you'll run it twice. The one-liner you can't reconstruct next week is a party trick; the saved script is a tool.

example.code:
# access log triage (Apache combined format)
awk '{print $1}' /var/log/apache2/access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10
awk '$9==404 {print $7}' /var/log/apache2/access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
# JSON logs: top 10 erroring endpoints
jq -r 'select(.status>=500) | .path' /var/log/app.json | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
example.walkthrough: The first pipeline finds the top talkers by IP — the brute-forcer or scraper stands out immediately. The second lists the most-requested 404 paths — vulnerability scanners probe `/wp-login`, `/.env`, `/admin` whether or not you run WordPress. The jq line does the same triage on JSON logs for 5xx endpoints. Three pipelines, three minutes, and you know what the internet wants from your server.

pitfalls: grep -c on huge logs without LC_ALL=C: multibyte locale handling makes grep 10x slower — set LC_ALL=C for byte-oriented log crunching.
One giant pipeline built blind: add one stage at a time, verifying output — debugging a 6-stage pipeline's empty output is miserable.
Never saving the pipeline: the triage you run every incident should be a script in the IR toolkit, not a memory exercise.
lessons.try_it: Against your lab's access logs (or generated sample data), find: top 5 IPs, top 10 404 paths, and any SQLi probe strings. Save the pipelines as scripts.

lessons.title: Password Hashing: bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2
concepts: Password storage has exactly one correct design: a slow, salted, memory-hard hash. MD5/SHA-256 are fast hashes — designed for speed, which is exactly what password crackers want (billions of guesses per second on a GPU). bcrypt, scrypt, and Argon2 are designed to be slow and memory-hungry — each guess costs real time and RAM, making brute force economically infeasible.

The salt: a unique random value per password, stored alongside the hash, that defeats rainbow tables (precomputed hash dictionaries). Without salts, one rainbow table cracks every identical password in the dump at once; with unique salts, each password must be attacked individually. The salt isn't secret — it's just unique.

Argon2id is the current recommendation (winner of the Password Hashing Competition, 2015): memory-hard, side-channel resistant, with tunable time/memory/parallelism. bcrypt remains perfectly respectable (and ubiquitous); scrypt is fine. The wrong answers are MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256-unsalted, and anything homebrewed — 'we hash with SHA-256 twice' is a finding, not a design.

Verification hygiene: use constant-time comparison for hashes (timing attacks on string comparison are real), set work factors so hashing takes ~0.5-1s (retune as hardware improves), and never cap password length below what the algorithm handles (bcrypt's 72-byte limit needs pre-hashing for long passphrases — document it).

example.code:
# Python: Argon2id via argon2-cffi (correct)
from argon2 import PasswordHasher
ph = PasswordHasher()  # Argon2id, sane defaults
hash = ph.hash('correct horse battery staple')
ph.verify(hash, 'correct horse battery staple')  # True
# WRONG (fast hash - crackable):
# hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest()
# WRONG (unsalted): same password -> same hash, rainbow-tableable
example.walkthrough: The correct code uses Argon2id with library defaults — memory-hard, salted automatically, verified with a constant-time compare inside the library. The commented wrong versions show the two classic failures: raw SHA-256 (GPU-crackable at billions/sec) and unsalted hashing (one rainbow table cracks all identical passwords). The difference is three lines and the entire security property.

pitfalls: Fast hashes for passwords: 'SHA-256 is secure' confuses collision-resistance with password-storage — speed is the enemy here; use memory-hard KDFs.
Homebrewed iterations ('SHA-256 10,000 times'): not memory-hard, probably buggy — use the reviewed algorithms.
Work factor from 2015: hardware got 10x faster, your bcrypt cost didn't — retune work factors periodically (≈1s per hash).
lessons.try_it: Hash a password with Argon2id and with SHA-256; time 1,000 verifications of each. The timing gap is the security property — write it up.

lessons.title: GPG: Encryption & Signing in Practice
concepts: GPG (GNU Privacy Guard) implements OpenPGP: public-key encryption ('only the key holder reads this') and digital signatures ('this provably came from the key holder'). The key pair: public key shared widely, private key guarded — ideally on a hardware token (YubiKey) so it can't be exfiltrated. Keyservers distribute public keys; the web of trust (or TOFU) authenticates them.

The practical workflows: encrypt a file for someone (`gpg --encrypt --recipient alice@example.com secrets.txt` — only Alice's private key decrypts it), sign a release (`gpg --detach-sign --armor release.tar.gz` — anyone with your public key verifies provenance), and encrypt-to-self for password stores (`pass`, the standard Unix password manager, is GPG-encrypted files in git).

Key hygiene: generate on the token when possible (private key never touches disk), set an expiry (a lost key without expiry is a forever-impersonation risk), publish revocation certificates securely, and back up the private key material offline before you need it. A GPG key without a backup is a future lockout; without revocation, a future impersonation.

The modern note: for most encryption needs, age (rage) is simpler than GPG; for signing, SSH keys (as in the git-devops signing lesson) or Sigstore are simpler. GPG remains the standard for email encryption, Debian package signing, and anywhere the OpenPGP ecosystem is entrenched — know it, but choose the simplest tool that fits.

example.code:
$ gpg --full-generate-key   # RSA 4096 or Ed25519, set expiry 2y
$ gpg --armor --export alice@example.com > alice.pub
$ gpg --encrypt --recipient alice@example.com plan.txt   # plan.txt.gpg
$ gpg --detach-sign --armor release-v1.4.0.tar.gz
$ gpg --verify release-v1.4.0.tar.gz.asc   # Good signature from Alice
example.walkthrough: The workflow covers the lifecycle: generate with an expiry (so a lost key eventually dies), export the public key for distribution, encrypt so only Alice reads it, detach-sign the release for provenance, and verify the signature — 'Good signature' is the cryptographic proof the release came from Alice's key. Each command is one half of a trust relationship.

pitfalls: No expiry on keys: a compromised key impersonates forever — set expiries and rotate; expiry is extendable while you hold the key.
Private key only on the laptop, no backup: laptop dies, identity dies with it — back up offline, ideally generated on hardware token.
Trusting keyserver keys blindly: keyservers don't verify identity — verify fingerprints out-of-band before trusting.
lessons.try_it: Generate a test GPG key, encrypt a file to yourself, sign a file, verify the signature, then practice revocation with a test key.

lessons.title: TLS Handshake & Certificate Chains
concepts: TLS is how the internet gets confidentiality, integrity, and authentication: the handshake negotiates the cipher suite, the server presents its certificate chain (leaf → intermediate → root), the client validates the chain against its trusted roots plus hostname matching, and then encrypted application data flows. Every padlock icon is this choreography.

The chain of trust: the leaf cert (your domain) is signed by an intermediate, signed by a root in the client's trust store. Serve the full chain (leaf + intermediates) — 'incomplete chain' is the most common TLS misconfiguration, breaking clients with strict validation while working in browsers that cache intermediates. `openssl s_client -showcerts` reveals what you actually serve.

The failure modes to recognize: expired certificates (monitoring! — the number of outages from expired certs is embarrassing industry-wide), hostname mismatch (cert for www, client asked for api), self-signed in production (no trust anchor), and weak configuration (TLS 1.0/1.1, RC4, no forward secrecy — test with testssl.sh or ssllabs.com).

For defenders: monitor expiry with alerting at 30/14/7 days (automate renewal with ACME/Let's Encrypt — manual renewal is the outage factory), scan your fleet's TLS configs on a schedule, and know that certificate transparency logs (from the recon domain) mean every cert you issue is public — don't put internal hostnames in public certs.

example.code:
$ echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com 2>/dev/null | \
    openssl x509 -noout -dates -issuer
dates: notBefore=..., notAfter=...   # check expiry!
issuer=C = US, O = Let's Encrypt
$ # full audit:
$ testssl.sh --fast example.com | grep -Ei 'protocol|grade'
example.walkthrough: The openssl pipeline extracts exactly the three things to check first: validity dates (is it expired or expiring?), and the issuer (is it the expected CA?). The testssl.sh line runs the deeper audit — protocol versions, cipher suites, known vulnerabilities — grading the configuration the way ssllabs.com does. Together they're the TLS health check for any endpoint.

pitfalls: Manual certificate renewal: the expiry outage is a rite of passage nobody should repeat — ACME automation (certbot) makes renewal a non-event.
Serving leaf-only chains: works in lenient browsers, breaks strict clients and APIs — always serve the full chain including intermediates.
Ignoring the expiry monitor: 30/14/7-day alerts are the standard — the outage from an expired cert is 100% preventable.
lessons.try_it: Audit three sites you use (or your lab's): check chain completeness, expiry dates, and protocol versions with testssl.sh or ssllabs.com. Write the findings.

lessons.title: Disk Imaging: dd & Write Blockers
concepts: Forensic imaging creates a bit-for-bit copy of storage without altering the original: the hardware write blocker sits between the drive and the workstation, physically preventing writes, while `dd` (or `dc3dd`/`ewfacquire` for forensic formats with built-in hashing) streams every sector — including deleted-file remnants in unallocated space — to the image file.

The order matters: document the drive (photos, serial numbers, labels), connect via write blocker, image, then hash both source and image (SHA-256) and compare — matching hashes prove the copy is exact and the source unaltered. Work only on the copy afterward; the original is sealed. Every deviation from this is a chain-of-custody argument for the defense.

Live vs dead imaging: powered-off drives image cleanly; live systems can't be frozen — files change during imaging, and memory (per the volatility order) must be captured first. For live systems, accept the inconsistency, document it, and prioritize: memory, then the most volatile disk data. 'Perfect' imaging of a running system is impossible; defensible imaging is the standard.

Volume reality: multi-terabyte drives take hours to image — plan for it (write speed, storage, hashing time), image the highest-value media first, and consider targeted collection (key directories + memory) when full-disk imaging isn't feasible. The perfect image you don't have time for loses to the targeted collection you complete.

example.code:
# forensic imaging workflow
# 1. document: photos, serial, labels
# 2. connect via hardware write blocker
$ sudo dc3dd if=/dev/sdb of=/evidence/case042.img hash=sha256 log=/evidence/case042.log
$ sha256sum /dev/sdb   # source hash (via blocker: reads fine)
$ sha256sum /evidence/case042.img   # must match
# 3. seal original, work only on the image (mount read-only loop
example.walkthrough: dc3dd improves on dd for forensics: built-in hashing during acquisition and a log file documenting the operation. The source and image hashes must match — that's the mathematical proof of an exact copy. The original is then sealed; all analysis happens on the image mounted read-only. Every step is documented because the image may one day be evidence.

pitfalls: Imaging without a write blocker: the OS may write (journal replays, automount) — the source is altered and the defense notices; block writes in hardware.
Working on the original: every analysis step modifies access times — image first, analyze the copy, seal the source.
No hashing: an unhashed image is just a file — hashes at acquisition prove integrity for every later handoff.
lessons.try_it: Practice on a USB stick: document it, image it with dd/dc3dd through a write blocker (or read-only mount as fallback), hash both, and verify the match.

lessons.title: Memory Forensics Basics
concepts: Memory holds what disk doesn't: running processes, network connections, encryption keys, injected code, and fileless malware that never touches the filesystem. The fileless attack lives entirely in RAM — no disk image will ever find it. Memory capture (LiME, winpmem, gcore) before power-off is what makes these investigations possible.

Volatility is the analysis framework: `vol.py -f mem.dump windows.pslist` lists processes, `netscan` shows connections, `malfind` finds injected code (memory regions with execute permission that don't map to files — the fileless signature), and `hashdump` extracts credential hashes. Each plugin answers one question; the investigation chains them.

The malfind signature deserves emphasis: legitimate code executes from files on disk; injected code executes from anonymous memory regions. `malfind` flags exactly that — executable memory with no file backing. It's the closest thing to a 'show me the malware' command in memory forensics, and the first plugin to run on a suspected fileless compromise.

The operational requirements: capture memory at the first sign of trouble (it degrades with every passing minute and vanishes at reboot), have the Volatility profiles for your OS versions ready before you need them, and practice — memory analysis is a perishable skill. The team that captures memory 'just in case' solves the fileless cases; the team that doesn't, doesn't.

example.code:
# memory forensics triage (Volatility 3)
$ vol -f mem.dump windows.pslist        # processes: look for odd parents/names
$ vol -f mem.dump windows.netscan       # connections: beaconing? C2?
$ vol -f mem.dump windows.malfind       # injected code <- fileless malware
$ vol -f mem.dump windows.hashdump      # credential material in memory
# odd parent (explorer.exe -> powershell.exe with no window) + malfind hit = investigate
example.walkthrough: The triage sequence narrows fast: process list for anomalies (wrong parents, masqueraded names), network connections for beaconing patterns, malfind for the fileless signature (executable anonymous memory), and hashdump for credential theft evidence. The comment shows the correlation that closes cases — process anomaly plus malfind hit is the fileless conviction.

pitfalls: Rebooting 'to clear the malware': destroys the only copy of fileless malware and all volatile evidence — capture memory first, always.
No Volatility profiles ready: analysis stalls while you build profiles for the exact OS build — prepare profiles for your fleet in advance.
Disk-only forensics on a fileless case: the image is clean because the malware was never on disk — memory is the crime scene.
lessons.try_it: In your lab, capture a process's memory with gcore, then practice Volatility basics on a sample image (Volatility's public samples) — run pslist and malfind.

lessons.title: Timeline Analysis
concepts: Timeline analysis reconstructs 'what happened, in order' from every timestamp on the system: filesystem MAC times (modified/accessed/changed), event logs, browser history, registry keys, and application logs — merged into one chronological super-timeline (Plaso/log2timeline is the standard tool). The incident narrative emerges from the ordering: the phish at 08:03, the payload at 08:07, lateral movement at 08:12.

MAC times are the filesystem's testimony: mtime (content modified), atime (accessed — often disabled for performance, know your systems), ctime (metadata changed — permissions, ownership). Attackers alter mtimes (timestomping) to blend in — but ctime can't be set arbitrarily on most systems, so ctime > mtime discrepancies expose the lie. The 'lying clock' scenario from forensics-intro is this in miniature.

The super-timeline workflow: collect the image, run Plaso against it, then filter the ocean — by time window (the incident window), by keyword (the attacker's tools, the targeted data), by anomaly (events at 3 AM, mass file access). The skill isn't generating the timeline (the tool does that) — it's knowing what to filter for.

Corroboration is the discipline: a single timestamp is a claim; three sources agreeing is a fact. The file's mtime says 08:07, the EDR shows process creation at 08:07, the firewall logs the C2 connection at 08:08 — now you have an event. Build the case the way you'd defend it: every key assertion backed by multiple sources.

example.code:
# Plaso super-timeline workflow
$ log2timeline.py --storage-file case.plaso /evidence/case042.img
$ psort.py -o l2tcsv -w timeline.csv case.plaso
# then filter: the incident window
$ grep '2026-10-0[89]' timeline.csv | grep -Ei 'mimikatz|psexec|sekurlsa' | head -20
# timestomp check: ctime newer than mtime on attacker tools
$ stat /evidence/mnt/Windows/Temp/svchost.exe
example.walkthrough: Plaso ingests the image into a single timeline database; psort exports it filterable. The grep narrows millions of events to the incident window and the attacker's known tools — the narrative in 20 lines. The stat check demonstrates timestomp detection: if ctime (metadata change) is newer than the claimed mtime, the timestamp was forged. Tools generate; analysts filter and corroborate.

pitfalls: Single-source conclusions: one timestamp is a claim — corroborate across filesystem, EDR, and network before asserting the narrative.
Ignoring ctime: attackers forge mtime routinely; ctime discrepancies are the tell — check both.
Timeline without a window: the full super-timeline is millions of rows — always bound by the incident window first, then expand.
lessons.try_it: On a lab image (or your own VM), run Plaso/log2timeline on a small partition, then practice: bound by a time window, filter by keyword, and corroborate one event across two sources.

lessons.title: Threat Modeling: STRIDE in Practice
concepts: Threat modeling asks 'what can go wrong?' before it does — systematically. STRIDE (Microsoft's mnemonic) enumerates threat classes per system element: Spoofing (fake identity), Tampering (data modification), Repudiation (denying actions), Information disclosure (leaks), Denial of service, Elevation of privilege. Walk each data flow through the six; the threats you name are the ones you can design against.

The process: draw the data-flow diagram (users, services, datastores, trust boundaries — the diagram is the model), apply STRIDE per element and flow, score the threats (DREAD or simple high/med/low), and convert each into a mitigation or an accepted risk with an owner. An unmodeled system is defended by hope; a modeled one by decisions.

The trust boundary is the key concept: every place data crosses from untrusted to trusted (user input to app, app to database, service to service) is where STRIDE applies hardest. Authentication at the boundary counters spoofing; authorization counters elevation; logging counters repudiation. The boundary diagram tells you where the controls go.

Threat modeling is a team sport done early: 90 minutes with the engineers who built it beats 90 days of pentesting the finished product for design flaws. Revisit when the architecture changes — the model rots as the system evolves, and a stale model is worse than none (it claims coverage it doesn't have).

example.code:
# STRIDE per data flow (login flow example)
user -> app (credentials):
  S: attacker spoofs user -> MFA, brute-force protection
  T: creds tampered in transit -> TLS
  R: user denies login attempt -> auth logging
  I: creds disclosed -> no logging of passwords, TLS
  D: login endpoint flooded -> rate limiting
  E: n/a (auth boundary itself)
app -> db (query):
  T: SQLi -> parameterized queries
  I: db creds in config -> secret manager
  E: app compromises db -> least-privilege db user
example.walkthrough: The worked example shows STRIDE applied to two flows: each threat class either yields a concrete mitigation or is marked not-applicable with reasoning. The app→db flow surfaces the SQLi and credential-storage threats that become the security requirements. This is the artifact: threats enumerated, each with a mitigation or an owner — design flaws caught before code exists.

pitfalls: Threat modeling the finished product: design flaws found post-build are 10x costlier — model at design time, when changes are cheap.
The model nobody updates: architecture evolved, threats didn't — re-model on significant changes or the coverage claim rots.
STRIDE as a checkbox: enumerating threats without scoring or owners produces a list nobody acts on — every threat gets a mitigation or a named accepted risk.
lessons.try_it: Threat-model a small app you know: draw the data flows, apply STRIDE to two flows, and write the top 3 threats with mitigations.

lessons.title: Defense in Depth: Layered Controls
concepts: Defense in depth assumes every control fails: the firewall will be bypassed, the phish will land, the vulnerability will be exploited — so you layer controls such that no single failure is total. The layers: perimeter (firewall, WAF, email filtering), network (segmentation, IDS), host (hardening, EDR), application (authz, input validation), data (encryption, backups). The attacker must defeat all of them; you must maintain all of them.

The Swiss-cheese model visualizes it: each layer is a slice with holes (weaknesses), but the holes don't align — the attack path through one layer's hole hits the next layer's cheese. Designing for non-alignment is the skill: don't put your only MFA on the same system as the password database; don't let the backup server share credentials with production.

Each layer buys something specific: prevention (stop the attack), detection (see the attack), and response (survive the attack). A layer cake of pure prevention with no detection means the bypass goes unnoticed for months — the Equifax pattern. Every critical asset needs all three properties across its layers.

Cost-effectiveness: layers have diminishing returns — the 8th firewall rule-set adds less than the first backup test. Invest in the missing layer categories first (most orgs lack detection and recovery, not prevention), and measure: red-team exercises test whether the layers actually compose, not just exist.

example.code:
# layer audit (per critical asset)
asset: customer database
  perimeter:  WAF + firewall (prevent) ......... present
  network:    DB in isolated VLAN (prevent) .... present
  host:       hardening + EDR (prevent+detect) . present
  app:        parameterized + authz (prevent) .. present
  data:       encryption at rest (prevent) ...... present
  detection:  DB query anomaly alerting ......... MISSING <- fix
  response:   tested restore from backup ........ MISSING <- fix
example.walkthrough: The layer audit reveals the common pattern: prevention layers all present, detection and response missing. The database is well-fortified but blind (no anomaly alerting on queries) and unrecoverable (untested restores). The audit format forces the question per asset per layer — and the missing rows are the prioritized investment plan.

pitfalls: Prevention-only layering: seven preventive controls, zero detection — the bypass lives undetected for months; every asset needs detect + respond too.
Correlated layers: firewall and WAF managed by the same misconfigured automation — one mistake kills both; diversify control planes.
Layers as checklist theater: controls exist but were never tested together — red-team to verify composition, not just presence.
lessons.try_it: Layer-audit one critical asset you manage using the format above. Identify the thinnest layer and write the fix as a project proposal.

lessons.title: Security Metrics That Matter
concepts: Most security metrics are vanity: 'attacks blocked' counts the noise the firewall was supposed to block; 'training completion' measures attendance, not behavior. Metrics that matter drive decisions: mean time to detect (MTTD) and respond (MTTR) — the two numbers that bound breach impact; patch latency for critical CVEs; phishing report rate; backup restore success rate; and the percentage of systems with EDR coverage.

The metric hierarchy: outcome metrics (MTTD/MTTR, breach count) tell you if security works; operational metrics (patch latency, MFA coverage) tell you why; activity metrics (scans run, tickets closed) tell you people are busy. Report outcomes upward, manage with operational metrics, and treat activity metrics as diagnostic — never as goals.

Goodhart's law stalks every metric: 'reduce MTTR' becomes 'close tickets fast without fixing'; 'reduce phish click rate' becomes 'send obvious phish.' Pair every metric with its gaming counterweight (MTTR + recurrence rate; click rate + report rate), and review metric definitions quarterly — the metric that can't be gamed hasn't been invented.

The board-level translation: executives don't need CVE counts, they need risk in business terms — 'our MTTD is 4 hours vs industry 21 days; a ransomware event costs us $X/hour; our tested restores bound recovery to Y hours.' Metrics that don't change a decision are trivia; find the decision each metric informs.

example.code:
# the metrics that matter (monthly review)
OUTCOME:    MTTD 3.2h | MTTR 7.8h | incidents: 2 (both contained)
OPERATIONAL: critical-patch p50: 6d | MFA coverage: 98% | EDR: 99%
             phish report rate: 34% (target 50%) | backup restore tests: 100%
DIAGNOSTIC: tickets closed: 412 | scans run: 30
# decision each drives: report rate -> training investment;
# patch p50 -> maintenance window policy; MTTR -> IR staffing
example.walkthrough: The dashboard separates outcome from operational from diagnostic metrics, and each line ends with the decision it drives — the anti-vanity test. The phish report rate below target justifies training investment; patch latency informs maintenance policy; MTTR trends justify IR staffing. Metrics without a decision are trivia; these all earn their place.

pitfalls: Vanity metrics as goals: 'attacks blocked' goes up when you're attacked more — it's not a success metric; measure outcomes (MTTD/MTTR).
Unpaired metrics: optimizing MTTR alone produces fast, shallow fixes — pair with recurrence rate to keep it honest.
Metrics nobody reviews: the dashboard emailed monthly and ignored — review cadence with decision owners, or don't bother collecting.
lessons.try_it: Pick three metrics from the list for an org you know, gather rough current values, and write the decision each would drive. Present it as a one-slide brief.

lessons.title: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: This bootcamp trains the security mindset through domains: Linux Hardening, Networking, Scripting, Crypto, Forensics, Recon & OSINT, Web Attacks, PrivEsc, Social Engineering, and Incident Response. Each domain has lessons (concepts with real commands and examples) and scenarios (decision drills simulating the judgment calls defenders make). Work them in order first; drill weak areas after.

The lesson anatomy: concepts build the mental model, the example shows real commands or configs with a walkthrough, pitfalls name the traps practitioners hit, and try-it gives you a hands-on exercise. Security is a doing discipline — the try-it reps in your own lab VMs are where knowledge becomes reflex.

Scenarios are the core assessment: each presents a realistic situation and asks for a decision, with the 'why' teaching the underlying principle. Attempt each scenario before reading the explanation — the retrieval effort is the learning. Restate the why in your own words; if you can't explain it, you don't own it.

Ethics and authorization are non-negotiable: every offensive technique here is taught for defense — to recognize, harden against, and investigate. Practice only on systems you own or have written authorization to test. 'I was just learning' is not a legal defense.

example.code:
# your study loop per domain
