1. read the lesson (concepts + example)
2. do the try-it in YOUR lab (owned/authorized systems only)
3. attempt the scenario BEFORE reading the why
4. restate the why in your own words
5. run the lab end-to-end
6. revisit weak scenarios in 3 days (spaced repetition)
example.walkthrough: The study loop makes each domain a repeatable routine: read, practice hands-on in your own lab, self-test on scenarios before peeking, restate the reasoning, run the lab, and space-repetition the weak spots. The authorization reminder is part of the loop — every technique here is practiced on owned or authorized systems, no exceptions.

pitfalls: Skipping lab practice: reading about Nmap is not the same as interpreting a scan — the hands-on reps build the reflex.
Practicing on unauthorized systems: the fastest way to turn learning into a legal incident — own it, lab it, or get it in writing.
Reading scenario answers first: the attempt-before-explanation is where the judgment forms — don't rob yourself of it.
lessons.try_it: Set up your lab this week: two VMs (attacker/defender or just targets) on an isolated network. Run the first domain's try-it exercises there.

lessons.title: Study Strategy for Linux Security
concepts: Security rewards the paranoid practitioner: weight your time toward hands-on reps — hardening a VM, reading a packet capture, triaging a log, writing a detector — at roughly 70/30 practice to theory. If you haven't done it in a lab, you don't know it; interviews will find the gap with one 'show me' question.

Build two artifacts as you go: a personal command reference (every Nmap phase, every Volatility plugin, every audit command — in your own words) and a findings journal (each lab's discoveries written as findings with severity and remediation). The reference becomes your interview cheat sheet; the journal becomes proof you think like an assessor.

Learn attack and defense as a pair: for every offensive technique (SQLi, privesc, phishing), know the detection and the fix. Interviewers ask 'how would you attack this?' to test whether you understand the defense — the candidate who answers with the full attack-defense pair demonstrates the mindset.

Reps under pressure: monthly, run a timed scenario drill — 45 minutes, mixed domains, no notes. Real incidents don't pause for Googling; the drill builds the calm that comes from having seen the pattern before. Review every miss with the full why, then re-drill it in a week.

example.code:
# weekly cadence
Mon/Wed/Fri: 1 new domain (lesson + try-it + scenarios)
Tue/Thu:     labs for the week's domains
Sat:         45-min timed mixed-domain drill
Sun:         review command reference + findings journal
# gate: 80%+ on last week's scenarios before advancing
example.walkthrough: The cadence alternates new material with consolidation: domains on alternate days, labs locking them in, a timed Saturday drill simulating incident pressure, and an 80% mastery gate before advancing. The two artifacts — command reference and findings journal — compound over the course into interview-ready proof of skill.

pitfalls: Theory-only studying: you can define XSS but can't find it in a lab app — the 'show me' interview question exposes this immediately.
Learning attacks without defenses: 'how would you attack this?' is a defense question in disguise — always learn the pair.
Skipping timed drills: knowledge without pressure-performance fails at 2 AM — the Saturday drill builds incident calm.
lessons.try_it: Start your command reference and findings journal today: enter the first domain's key commands and one finding written with severity and remediation.

lessons.title: Course Map: From Hardening to Incident Response
concepts: The course follows the attack lifecycle in reverse — defense first, then the attacker's view, then response. Foundations: Linux Hardening, Networking Security, Scripting, Crypto Basics — the ground every defender stands on. You can't investigate what you can't see, and you can't see without logging, networking, and crypto fundamentals.

Attacker's view: Recon & OSINT, Web App Attacks, PrivEsc & Persistence, Social Engineering — how adversaries actually get in and stay in. This knowledge is defensive: every technique maps to a detection and a hardening action. You learn the attack to kill the attack.

Response: Forensics Intro and Incident Response — what happens when prevention fails. Triage, containment, eradication, evidence handling: the disciplines that bound the damage. The capstone integrates all three phases into a full assessment-and-response exercise.

Defensive Mindset threads through everything: threat modeling, defense in depth, metrics. It's the senior layer — the difference between a technician who runs tools and a practitioner who designs security. Interviews for senior roles live in this layer.

example.code:
foundations:  hardening -> networking -> scripting -> crypto
attack view:  recon/osint -> web attacks -> privesc/persistence -> social eng
response:     forensics -> incident response
thread:       defensive mindset (threat modeling, depth, metrics)
capstone:     full assessment + response exercise
example.walkthrough: The map mirrors reality: defenders harden first, then learn the adversary's playbook to know what they're defending against, then learn response for when defenses fail. The arrows are dependencies — web-attack defense assumes networking knowledge; forensics assumes logging fundamentals. The capstone at the end exercises the full arc: assess, attack (authorized), detect, respond.

pitfalls: Skipping foundations for the 'exciting' attack domains: privesc technique without Linux fundamentals is trivia — the map's order builds the base first.
Treating incident response as optional: prevention eventually fails for everyone — response is where careers are made.
Ignoring the mindset thread: tool operators are common; practitioners who threat-model and measure are hired.
lessons.try_it: Draw the course map from memory and place each domain. For any domain you can't place, read its first lesson before continuing.

lessons.title: Assessment & Interview Strategy
concepts: Security interviews test judgment under three formats: scenarios ('you find a web shell — first three actions?'), live labs ('harden this VM in 30 minutes' / 'find the vulnerability in this app'), and mindset questions ('how do you prioritize 500 vulnerabilities?'). This bootcamp's scenarios train the first, labs the second, defensive-mindset the third.

For scenario answers, use: contain first (stop the bleeding), scope second (how big is it?), preserve evidence third, then eradicate and recover. Narrate the ordering — 'I'd isolate before investigating because...' — because interviewers score the prioritization, not just the action list. The IR lifecycle is your answer skeleton.

For live labs, narrate your methodology: 'I'm checking SUID binaries first because that's the fastest privesc path; then sudoers; then capabilities.' Methodology narration turns tool output into evidence of structured thinking. And always state authorization boundaries unprompted — 'in a real engagement I'd confirm scope before scanning' signals professionalism.

For 'tell me about a time,' mine your labs: 'In my capstone I found the same SUID misconfiguration three ways — LinPEAS flagged it, my manual find confirmed it, and the fix was a config-management change fleet-wide.' Specific, methodical, and quantified beats generic every time.

example.code:
# scenario answer skeleton (say it out loud)
1. contain: stop the bleeding (isolate, block, disable)
2. scope: how big? (expand from indicators)
3. preserve: evidence before eradication
4. eradicate + recover: remove cause, restore phased
5. learn: postmortem, playbook update
# live lab narration: 'checking X first because Y' - methodology aloud
example.walkthrough: The five-step skeleton (contain → scope → preserve → eradicate/recover → learn) is the speaking framework for incident scenarios — it demonstrates prioritization under pressure. The live-lab note captures the differentiator: narrating methodology ('checking X first because Y') shows structured thinking, and stating authorization boundaries unprompted signals the professionalism security roles require.

pitfalls: Action lists without ordering: 'I'd check logs, isolate, patch...' in random order scores poorly — the skeleton's ordering IS the judgment.
Silent live labs: tool output without methodology looks like luck — narrate why each check comes first.
Skipping the authorization mention: in security interviews, unprompted scope-awareness is a hiring signal — state it.
lessons.try_it: Take one incident scenario and answer it aloud with the five-step skeleton. Then take a hardening lab and narrate your check ordering as you work.

lessons.title: Capstone Architecture: The Range You'll Build
concepts: The capstone range is a small virtual network: two target VMs (a Linux web server with intentional misconfigurations, a workstation), an attacker Kali VM, and a defender/logging VM (SIEM-ish log aggregation). Everything runs isolated — host-only networking, no internet route for the targets. The range is the lab that the whole course has been preparing you for.

The target VMs are deliberately vulnerable in documented ways: SUID misconfigurations, weak sudoers, an outdated web app with SQLi/XSS, exposed services, credential material in history files, and a phishing-prone 'user' persona. You build the vulnerabilities from a checklist — building them teaches the misconfiguration patterns better than just exploiting them.

The defender VM centralizes logging (rsyslog + auditd forwarding from targets), runs the monitoring queries you'll write (failed logins, new SUID binaries, persistence changes), and hosts your IR toolkit (Velociraptor or scripts, Volatility, Plaso). The range thus exercises both halves: the attacker's path and the defender's visibility.

Rules of engagement (write them down): isolated network only, no testing outside the range, snapshot before destructive phases, and a findings journal from day one. The ROE document is itself a deliverable — it demonstrates the professionalism assessors are hired for.

example.code:
# capstone range topology (host-only, isolated)
[attacker: kali] --\n[defender: logs + IR toolkit] -- [target-web: LAMP, vuln app, misconfigs]
                             \-- [target-ws: workstation, user persona]
# logging: targets forward auditd + syslog -> defender VM
# snapshots: before recon, before exploitation, before IR phase
example.walkthrough: The topology shows the four-VM range on an isolated host-only network: attacker, defender/log aggregator, and two targets with documented vulnerabilities. The logging arrows are the defender's visibility; the snapshots are the safety net for destructive phases. The ROE note makes explicit what the whole bootcamp has implied — isolated, documented, professional.

pitfalls: Internet-routed targets: the vulnerable VMs must never touch the internet — host-only networking, verified, before any exploitation.
Building the range without the logging VM: you get the attack reps but none of the detection reps — the defender VM is half the capstone.
No snapshots: ransomware-phase without a rollback plan turns the capstone into a rebuild weekend — snapshot at every phase boundary.
lessons.try_it: Draw your range topology, list the intentional vulnerabilities per target (10+), and write your one-page ROE. Get the network isolation verified before building.

lessons.title: Capstone Build Guide: Assess, Harden, Respond
concepts: Phase 1 — Assess (attacker view, authorized by your own ROE): passive recon on the range, Nmap phased scans, web app testing (SQLi, XSS, IDOR), privesc enumeration (SUID, sudo, creds), and a social-engineering tabletop against the 'user' persona. Document every finding with severity, evidence, and remediation — this is the findings journal, the assessor's core artifact.

Phase 2 — Harden (defender view): fix every Phase 1 finding — SSH hardening, firewall rules, remove SUID bits, fix sudoers, parameterize the app's queries, add security headers, deploy auditd + forwarding, segment the range network. Re-run the Phase 1 assessment and confirm the findings are closed: the before/after is the proof the hardening worked.

Phase 3 — Incident response (the twist): with the hardened range, your partner (or a script) introduces a compromise — a web shell, a phished credential, a persistence mechanism. You detect (your monitoring should fire), triage, contain, eradicate, recover, and write the postmortem. The detection firing is the grade for Phase 2's monitoring.

Verification at each gate: Phase 1 ends with a findings report reviewed against the vulnerability checklist (did you find all 10+?); Phase 2 ends with a clean re-assessment; Phase 3 ends with a timeline, a postmortem, and updated playbooks. Gates keep the capstone honest — no advancing on vibes.

example.code:
# phase gates
PHASE 1 (assess): findings journal with 10+ vulns, each: severity,
            evidence, remediation. Gate: reviewed vs checklist.
PHASE 2 (harden): all findings remediated; re-assessment clean.
            Gate: before/after evidence per finding.
PHASE 3 (respond): injected compromise -> detected via YOUR
            monitoring -> full IR lifecycle -> postmortem.
            Gate: timeline + postmortem + playbook updates.
example.walkthrough: The three phases form the complete arc with a gate at each transition: assessment produces the findings journal, hardening produces before/after evidence, and response produces the timeline and postmortem. The Phase 3 twist — the compromise is injected into your hardened range — tests whether your monitoring actually detects, which is the honest grade for all of Phase 2's work.

pitfalls: Skipping the findings journal: the assessment without documentation is entertainment — the journal is the deliverable that proves assessor thinking.
Hardening without re-assessment: 'I think I fixed it' is the vulnerability that survives — re-run the attacks to prove closure.
Phase 3 without Phase 2's monitoring: nothing fires, and the IR phase becomes a scavenger hunt — the detection grade is earned in Phase 2.
lessons.try_it: Complete Phase 1 this week: build the two targets from your vulnerability checklist, run the assessment, and write the findings journal. Don't harden anything yet.

lessons.title: Capstone Report & Portfolio Packaging
concepts: The final report is the portfolio artifact: executive summary (risk in business terms), methodology (what you did, in what order, under what ROE), findings (each with severity, evidence, remediation, and before/after for fixed items), the incident timeline from Phase 3, and the postmortem with action items. Write it for a hiring manager who wasn't in the room.

The demo: a 10-minute narrated walkthrough — the range topology, one attack path end-to-end (recon → exploit → privesc), the hardening that closed it (before/after), and the Phase 3 detection firing on the injected compromise with the IR timeline. Live or recorded, narrated throughout: methodology aloud is what separates practitioners from tool-runners.

Quantify everything: 'found 14 vulnerabilities across 6 classes,' 'MTTD on the injected compromise: 8 minutes via my auditd alert,' 'hardening closed 14/14 on re-assessment.' Numbers make the judgment legible. Include the ROE and note the authorization boundary explicitly — employers in security hire for trustworthiness as much as skill.

Publish responsibly: the report lives in your portfolio with sensitive details generalized (no working exploit code against real products, no target-identifying specifics beyond your lab). A sanitized public report plus 'full version available on request' is the professional standard — it proves skill without arming anyone.

example.code:

1. executive summary (risk in business terms, 1 page)
2. methodology + ROE (what, in what order, under what authority)
3. findings (severity, evidence, remediation, before/after)
4. phase 3: detection timeline + IR narrative
5. postmortem + playbook updates
6. appendix: command reference used
# demo (10 min): topology -> attack path -> hardening proof ->
#                 detection firing -> IR timeline
example.walkthrough: The report structure serves two audiences: the executive summary translates to business risk, the methodology and findings prove practitioner rigor. The demo script moves through the arc in 10 minutes — attack path, hardening proof, detection firing, IR timeline — with methodology narrated throughout. The responsible-publishing note is the trust signal security employers screen for.

pitfalls: Publishing working exploits: the portfolio should prove judgment, not distribute weapons — sanitize, generalize, offer details on request.
Report without the ROE: no stated authorization boundary reads as no boundary — the ROE is a trust signal, include it.
No quantification: 'did security stuff' vs '14 findings, 8-minute MTTD, 14/14 closed' — numbers are what hiring managers remember.
lessons.try_it: Draft your report's executive summary now (one page, business risk language) — even before the range is built. It focuses the whole capstone.

items: Bash safety — verifying a published checksum or signature (fetched separately) before executing is the minimum due diligence. curl|bash as a habit trains you to execute uninspected code as root — the exact behavior attackers rely on.

Idempotent scripts — automation that isn't idempotent becomes a liability: duplicate firewall rules, failed user creation, unpredictable state. Cron's minimal environment (bare PATH, no shell profile) breaks scripts that work interactively — absolute paths fix that.

sections.heading: Cryptography Basics
items: Password hashing — hashing proves integrity and identity (this file hasn't changed); encryption provides confidentiality (only key holders can read).

Storage security — an attacker can sign anything with their own key; the security is in the key distribution (verified fingerprint, trusted introducer, prior secure exchange). Using the wrong primitive means the security property you wanted doesn't exist.
Hashing vs encryption — this confusion causes real design failures: hashed backups are still readable by everyone (hashing doesn't hide data); 'encrypted' passwords are recoverable.
Key management — real systems are hybrid: asymmetric crypto (slow, solves key distribution) exchanges a random symmetric key; symmetric crypto (fast) encrypts the bulk data.
Common trap — hashing is encryption with a fixed key.
Common trap — use the current timestamp as the key.

sections.heading: Forensics Intro
items: Order of volatility — forensics discipline: preserve (memory first per order of volatility, then disk image), document the chain of custody, and analyze copies. Order of volatility governs triage: registers/cache → memory → network state → running processes → disk → logs → backups.

Evidence preservation — every action on a live suspect system alters evidence — and rebooting destroys memory-resident artifacts entirely. Evidence is only as strong as its handling story: cryptographic hashes prove the image hasn't changed since collection, contemporaneous notes…
File timestamps — one timestamp is a claim; corroborated timestamps are evidence.

Timestomping — the mismatch is the tell: atime/mtime are trivially set with touch, but ctime (inode change time) updates on any metadata change and can't be set arbitrarily — today's ctime exposes the timestomping.
File recovery — recovery means: stop writing to that disk immediately (image it), carve the image for log-format data, and check log forwarding/SIEM copies (attackers forget the remote copy).

items: Attack path thinking — defensive prioritization maps attack paths to crown jewels (internet → DMZ → creds → domain) and breaks the chains at the cheapest links (MFA, segmentation, patching the pivot points).
Prioritization — cVE-count prioritization burns weeks on unreachable printers while the domain falls.
Assume breach — every major breach involved a bypassed perimeter — phishing, vendor access, misconfig.
Least privilege — assume-breach doesn't mean defeat; it means designing so one failure isn't total: segmentation contains, internal monitoring detects, least privilege limits blast radius.
